articles.title: Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
articles.text:
Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
Cutting back on salt may not be enough to get the greatest benefits for blood pressure.
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- University of Vermont
- Summary:
- Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.
- Share:
For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.
Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.
The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.
Why Potassium Matters for Blood Pressure
Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.
Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.
In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.
"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."
A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines
The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.
The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.
One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.
Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.
This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.
How to Get More Potassium in Your Diet
Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.
Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.
However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.
Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.
A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure
The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.
The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."
For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.
The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Vermont. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Naomi K Fukagawa, Paul A Welling, Janice Johnson, Kristin Reimers, Soo-Yeun Lee, Patricia Zecca. Rethinking the impact of dietary sodium and potassium on blood pressure to advance public health. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2026; 124 (2): 101396 DOI: 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2026.101396

articles.title: A 35mm lens with an f/1.8 aperture — and under $400? Viltrox delivers
articles.text:
Space Verdict
The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) is an impressive lens for the price and certainly won’t break the bank. Image quality is impressive but imperfect, yet it's still an attractive lens.
Reasons to buy
- + Enticing price
- + Manual aperture ring
- + Impressive image quality
Reasons to avoid
- - Vignetting wide open
- - Some astigmatism at the frame edges
- - Only available in two lens mounts
Why you can trust Space.com
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.
Type: Full-frame prime lens
Focal length: 35 mm
Maximum aperture: f/1.8
Lens mount: Sony FE & Nikon Z
Weight: 12.52 oz / 355 g
Dimensions: 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm
Filter thread: 58 mm
Release date: April 2026
Budget primes can be, surprisingly, excellent choices for photographers shooting all subjects. It’s all too easy to get carried away with the best specs, such as a large maximum aperture and impressive optical design often seen in more expensive options. But affordable lenses like the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) have the potential to impress and delight in equal measure.
The 35mm f/1.8 is a compact and lightweight lens offering a reasonably fast maximum aperture, making it a prime candidate for astrophotography. It’s also the same size and almost the same weight as the Viltrox AF 55mm f/1.8 FE (APO), another lens that could potentially grace your camera bag.
With a highly attractive price tag of just $399 / £385, and mount options for Nikon Z and Sony FE, many astrophotographers will be wondering if this is a lens worth considering. It features 13 elements in 10 groups, as well as featuring an apochromatic (APO) design for reducing chromatic aberration as much as possible. As much as possible is key here because not all lenses are as successful as the manufacturer claims, although that’s not a comment on the 35mm f/1.8. Read on to discover if this could be one of the best lenses for astrophotography.
Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review
Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): Performance
- Sharp images for the price
- Sweet spot at f/8-f/11, not ideal for astro
- Some astigmatism at the edges of the frame
For a budget lens, the 35mm f/1.8 produces great, yet not perfect, image quality. On the plus side, images are nice and sharp, particularly in the centre, even when shooting wide open at f/1.8. At this aperture setting, though, there is some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. This is a surprise since it’s an APO lens, and, equally surprising, it’s isolated, but it is something you have to consider.
You do have to zoom into the image to see it, so it may not be a dealbreaker. Photos shot at f/1.8 are sharpest in the centre, with some fall-off towards the edges, with the corners exhibiting the least sharpness. There’s also the strongest vignetting at f/1.8. At the time of writing, there’s no Adobe Lightroom lens profile for the lens, but you can manually remove the vignetting and even create a preset of your own.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The vignette disappears as soon as f/4, with a gradual increase in sharpness across the frame between f/2.8 and f/5.6. f/8 and f/11 appear identical in terms of sharpness and occupy the sweet spot, while diffraction is clearly at work when you stop down to f/16. In reality, it’s unlikely you’d shoot beyond f/11 with this lens, even if you were shooting landscapes.
Overall, image quality is impressive despite not being perfect and stopping down to f/2.8 when shooting astro does provide greater clarity across the frame. This is, as you know, at the expense of having to shoot at a slightly higher ISO setting to compensate.
Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): Design
- Compact and lightweight
- Manual aperture ring
- Weather sealed
While f/1.8 lenses may not have the speed and light-gathering capabilities of faster f/1.4 and f/1.2 lenses, they’re considerably smaller and lighter. The lens only has a 58mm filter thread, so if you use any night filters, they will be at the less expensive end of the price scale.
For some photographers, the slight speed reduction of f/1.8 is a worthy compromise, and at 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm with a weight of 12.52 oz / 355 g, the 35mm f/1.8 is beautifully compact and balances well with camera bodies.
Build quality is excellent, and it’s fair to say the lens belies its budget price tag. The metal build alongside the manual aperture ring gives the 35mm f/1.8 a much more premium look and feel.
The aperture ring can also be set to A for in-body aperture adjustments, as well as offering the ability to switch the aperture click on and off. The latter is most popular with videographers. There’s also a customizable Fn button on the side.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The lens is weather-sealed against light rain and dust, with a rubber gasket on the lens mount. The front element also features a water and smudge-resistant coating, which is certainly useful for outdoor photography. Plus, there’s a minimum focusing distance of just 13.4 in / 34 cm, which is useful for daylight photography but of no consequence for astrophotography.
The 35mm f/1.8 is made up of 13 elements in 10 groups, and as previously mentioned, features an APO design, which is intended to eliminate chromatic aberration in high-contrast scenes.
The elements include two extra-low dispersion (ED), three high refractive index (HR) and one ultra aspherical (UA). The UA lens is claimed to be Viltrox’s LAB Series quality, which matches the Viltrox flagship line-up.
Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): Functionality
- Smooth manual focus
- Internal focusing
- Stepping motor-powered AF
When it comes to features, prime lenses are always pretty basic, with few features to shout about. The 35mm f/1.8 is certainly no exception, but its build quality and overall design hold up alongside its image quality and reasonably fast maximum aperture. It does, however, have a few points worth mentioning.
One feature that many Viltrox lenses have, including the 35mm f/1.8, is a USB-C Port on the lens mount. This allows you to use a smartphone app or a desktop app to quickly and easily update firmware. This is so much easier than having to download a file to your memory card and installing lens updates via the camera, which is how most native lenses have to be updated.
The manual aperture ring features click and clickless operation via a switch on the side, so you can easily see what aperture you’re using at a glance. The focusing ring is smooth and offers comfortable resistance, making manual focus a breeze. It’s also wide enough to rotate using gloves, although, being a compact lens, it’s narrower than what you’d expect on a larger and faster prime lens.
Autofocus (AF) is reasonably fast and silent, being powered by an stepping motor (STM). The AF performance seemed to improve after the firmware update that was installed via the desktop app before testing fully commenced.
This functionality isn’t, of course, relevant to astrophotography, but it’s still a useful point to mention in case you intend to use the lens with autofocus in the day. Focusing is also internal, so the front element doesn’t rotate during focusing like cheap and cheerful kit lenses.
How we tested the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO)
The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) was tested with the Sony A7R V, which offers an unforgivingly high resolution. The lens was tested at night with a focus on astrophotography, and in daylight to assess sharpness, distortion and general functionality for an all-round approach to testing.
Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): User reviews
Online reviews echo one another, praising the AF 35mm f/1.8 for its sharpness and cost. Users appreciate that while it’s certainly not in the league of Sony’s premium G Master lenses, it represents great value for money. Some reviewers mention great build quality and looking good when paired with their Sony camera.
Should you buy the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO)?
✅ You’re on a tight budget: The price of this lens is extremely attractive given the specs and performance.
✅ You want portability: This is a compact and lightweight lens that's much less bulky than faster primes.
❌ You want the best: This is a great little lens in many ways, but its image quality isn't the best that money can buy.
❌ You shoot APS-C: Unless this is what you want, the equivalent focal length on a crop sensor is 52.5mm
Prime lenses can be expensive, especially if you’re looking at those with an f/1.4 or f/1.2 maximum aperture. The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) is a budget option in the Viltrox line-up, but with decent overall performance alongside impressive image quality for the price, this is a great 35mm lens for those on a budget. It’s also compact and lightweight, which could be useful if you often head out shooting with several lenses in your kit bag.
Just going back to image quality, images are sharp, but when shooting astrophotography at f/1.8, there was some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. You can only really see this when you zoom in to 100%, but it’s worth bearing in mind if you’re looking for the closest to optical perfection you can find.
When a weather-sealed prime lens with a manual aperture ring costs just $399 / £385, you can’t help but take notice. Build quality is excellent and the lens undoubtedly looks and feels like it would be more expensive than it is.
Considering all of this and the image quality, the lens is fairly priced and is still at the release price, so it could become more affordable in the future. Just like other Viltrox lenses, in the box you get the lens, a lens hood, front and rear lens caps and a soft lens case.
If this lens isn't for you
The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.2 LAB FE is part of Viltrox’s flagship lens series and offers a much faster maximum aperture, as the name suggests. It’s also more expensive, larger and heavier.
If you’d like a wider lens, the Sony FE 20mm f/1.8 G is a fantastic option offering exceptional image quality alongside a compact build and light weight. A potential must-have for Sony users.
If you’d like to go wider still, the Sigma 14mm f/1.4 DG DN Art is an absolute beast of a lens, offering an ultra-wide light-gathering field of view alongside a fast f/1.4 maximum aperture.
James is an award-winning freelance landscape and portrait photographer, as well as a highly experienced photography journalist working with some of the best photography magazines and websites with a worldwide audience. He’s also the author of The Digital Darkroom: The Definitive Guide to Photo Editing. www.jamesaphoto.co.uk

articles.title: New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss
articles.text:
New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.
- Share:
An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.
The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.
Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.
Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.
A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity
Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.
That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.
The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.
At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.
The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.
The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.
How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar
The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.
Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.
The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.
A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.
The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.
Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.
Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice
To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.
The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.
The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.
Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.
"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.
Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.
Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?
Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.
"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."
The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.
The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.
Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.
One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.
Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.
If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Debasis Maity, Preetam Guha Ray, Peter Buchmann, Ghislaine Charpin-El Hamri, Martin Fussenegger. Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity. Science, 2026; 394 (6822) DOI: 10.1126/science.ady8560

articles.title: JWST uncovers new clues about the origins of 'interstellar invader' comet 3I/ATLAS
articles.text:
James Webb Space Telescope uncovers new clues about the origins of 'interstellar invader' comet 3I/ATLAS
The findings are another clue towards understanding the origins of 3I/ATLAS and the planet-forming conditions around other stars.
Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), scientists have found that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was built from tiny grains of ice mixed with dust that are quite different from the solar system’s comets.
These ice grains do, however, bear striking similarities to some icy bodies located at the edge of the solar system, beyond the orbit of Neptune, so-called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs).
3I/ATLAS was discovered entering the solar system in the summer of 2025. It was only the third object found entering the solar system from farther afield in the Milky Way after 1I/'Oumuamua, seen in 2017, and 2I/Borisov, detected in 2019. This meant the interstellar comet offered a rare chance to glimpse the conditions under which such bodies form in other star systems. Thus, the JWST was quickly on the trail of 3I/ATLAS.
"We designed [JWST] to be ready the moment an active interstellar comet was found and to follow it over time," Martin Cordiner of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America said in a statement.
Cordiner leads the JWST program to study objects such as 3I/ATLAS, and he is a co-author on a new research paper describing some of the findings.
The unclear origins of 3I/ATLAS
Researchers know that 3I/ATLAS wasn't born in the solar system, but nobody knows around which star 3I/ATLAS formed. What scientists are more sure of is the fact that this interstellar comet was produced within a planet-forming disk of gas and dust around a young star, possibly as long ago as 10 to 12 billion years. That's over twice the age of our solar system. It was then ejected from its home system somehow and left to wander interstellar space before encountering our solar system.
Like the familiar comets in our solar system, 3I/ATLAS is composed of grains of ice less than a micron – a millionth of a meter – in size. When the surface of the comet is warmed by the sun, gas erupts outwards, carrying ice grains into the cloud of ice and dust surrounding the comet, its coma, and its tail, where JWST can detect them.
When viewed spectroscopically, the water-ice in comets native to our solar system creates a strong absorption line in a comet’s spectrum at a wavelength of three microns, as well as less-prominent absorption lines at 1.5 and two microns.
Yet when the JWST’s Near-Infrared spectrograph (NIRSpec) instrument viewed 3I/ATLAS three times between August 2025, before its closest approach to the sun, and after closest approach in April 2026, scientists found the 1.5- and two micron absorption lines were missing, though the three-micron line remained strong.
"That combination was a puzzle," research lead author Silvia Protopapa of the South-west Research Institute said. "The strong three-micron band points to water-ice in the coma, but the weak or absent shorter-wavelength bands suggest the ice is not in the form we usually see in solar system comets."
The JWST's muddy 3I/ATLAS findings
Whenever presented with an unusual observational signature such the JWST delievered for 3I/ATLAS researchers turn to modeling to find the physical characteristics that best fit the spectrum. 
The modeling suggested to Protopapa’s team that 3I/ATLAS was composed of sub-micron grains of dirty water-ice, rich in dust. In comparison, the grains from the solar system’s indigenous comets are much cleaner, with almost pure water-ice relatively uncontaminated by dust.
"What seems to set [3I/ATLAS’ grains] apart is how much dust is mixed into the ice," said Protopapa. "Those grains hold clues to the conditions where the comet was born."
Comets are made of primordial material found in the planet-forming disk of gas and dust that surrounds a young star, and therefore the composition of comets can provide a window into the conditions in which planets form.
Whereas solar system comets tell us about the birth of Earth, an interstellar comet can tell us about conditions in which planets formed around another star, and how similar or dissimilar those conditions were to the birth of the solar system.
Yet comets are not the only icy remnants that date back to such primordial times. There are various families of bodies in the outer solar system, and 3I/ATLAS’ spectrum bears a resemblance to the spectrum of some medium-sized TNOs that are rich in carbon-dioxide ice and organic compounds (organic meaning containing carbon atoms). Indeed, in a separate 2025 study led by Cordiner, the JWST found 3I/ATLAS to have one of the greatest abundances of carbon dioxide ever seen in a comet.
TNOs are sizable bodies that are located far beyond the orbit of Neptune, The TNOs in question would have formed in a different part of the Sun’s protoplanetary disk than most comets and their composition reflects that.
On the other hand, the results imply that 3I/ATLAS was formed around its star of origin from similar icy material to that which produced some of the TNOs in our solar system, showing that the building blocks of planets around other stars share a common range of properties with the building blocks that formed our solar system. Indeed, 3I/ATLAS could even be a fragment of a TNO-like body that was shattered in a collision.
"At first glance, 3I/ATLAS looks different from the icy comets we know," said Protopapa. "But when we placed it alongside distant icy worlds in our own solar system, it no longer looked out of place. 
"This suggests that the icy building block of planets, here and around other stars, may share ice in the form of tiny, micron-scale grains, ranging from relatively pure ice to ice mixed with dust, with 3I/ATLAS toward the dusty end."
What this tells us is that these sub-micron-sized icy grains must form first in planet-forming disks, to then be incorporated into large bodies such as comets and protoplanets.
The team's findings were published on Monday (Oct. 26) in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

articles.title: Loài vật quý hiếm tưởng tuyệt chủng bất ngờ "tái xuất" trong vườn nhà dân
articles.text:
Một loài gà quý hiếm đã tuyệt chủng trong tự nhiên bất ngờ được phát hiện đang lang thang quanh một khu vườn nhà dân.
Gà lôi Lady Amherst được du nhập vào Anh từ Trung Quốc vào thế kỷ 19 và không có báo cáo nào về việc nhìn thấy loài gà này kể từ năm 2019.
Gà lôi Lady Amherst.
Nhưng sinh viên Sophie Pearson, 23 tuổi, đã vô cùng sửng sốt khi nhìn thấy loài gà lộng lẫy này đi ngang qua cửa sổ nhà cô ở St Andrews, Fife.
Gà lôi Lady Amherst trống trưởng thành có chiều dài 100-120cm. Trong khi đó, chiều dài đuôi chiếm 80cm chiều dài cơ thể của nó. Con mái nhỏ hơn con trống đôi chút.
Chúng có bộ lông màu trắng pha đen, mào đỏ. Đuôi của giống gà này có màu xám với 2 chõm lông màu đỏ. Gà trống có màu sắc sặc sỡ hơn gà mái. Lông của gà mái chủ yếu là màu đốm nâu nhạt. Chân của gà lôi Lady Amherst có màu xám.
Thức ăn của gà lôi Lady Amherst là các loạt hạt ngũ cốc, rau, cỏ, động vật không xương sống. Loài gà này bay rất kém. Tuy nhiên khi giật mình nó có thể bay khá xa. Con trống thường dùng âm thanh và bộ lông sặc sỡ của mình để đi dụ dỗ bạn tình.
Hiện tại, gà lôi Lady Amherst đã được Liên minh Bảo tồn Thiên nhiên Quốc tế (IUCN) đưa vào sách đỏ.

articles.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
articles.text:
Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- McGill University
- Summary:
- In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice.
The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive.
"There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute.
"Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail.
Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature.
Why Unhealthy Diets Produced Surprising Results
One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment.
"Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise."
However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans.
Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective.
A New Explanation for Cancer's Obesity Paradox
The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox."
Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods.
These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system.
By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity.
About the Study
The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators.
Funding was provided by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Terry Fox Research Institute, the Canada Foundation for Innovation, and philanthropic supporters including La Vie en Rose and the Bachynski Family Foundation.

articles.title: Nông dân Australia bắt được "quái vật" hơn 100 năm chưa từng xuất hiện và từng được cho là đã tuyệt chủng
articles.text:
Loài này được cho là đã tuyệt chủng ở Nam Úc và không có ghi chép chính thức nào trong khoảng hơn 100 năm qua. Tuy nhiên nó đã được phát hiện lại một lần nữa bởi một người nông dân sau khi thấy đàn gà của mình dần biến mất một cách bí ẩn.
Bạn có ngạc nhiên nếu bắt được một con vật đã không được nhìn thấy hàng trăm năm không? Một nông dân ở Úc, gần đây đã thấy rằng đàn gà của anh thường xuyên mất tích nên đã đặt bẫy để truy tìm thủ phạm. Ban đầu, anh ta tưởng thủ phạm bắt gà của mình là một con mèo hoặc một loài động vật phiền toái khác nhưng khi kiểm tra bẫy, anh ta phát hiện ra mình đã bắt được một con vật lạ có răng nanh mà mình chưa được nhìn thấy bao giờ.
Anh nói với truyền thông địa phương: "Tôi tưởng sẽ tìm thấy một con mèo hoang, nhưng tôi lại tìm thấy con vật nhỏ này. Thật không thể tin được". Trên thực tế, loài vật này đã được ghi nhận là tuyệt chủng tại Nam Úc từ những năm 1880, cách đây hơn 100 năm. Ở thời điểm hiện tại, sau khi phát hiện ra cá thể của loài này, chính quyền địa phương đang tích cực tìm kiếm thêm những con mèo túi đuôi đốm khác để tiền hành các biện pháp bảo tồn.
Mèo túi đuôi đốm là một trong nhiều loài thú có túi độc đáo không được tìm thấy ở nơi nào khác ngoại trừ ở Úc và New Guinea. Giống như nhiều loài thú có túi khác, bao gồm cả chuột túi, sự tiến hóa của mèo túi đuôi đốm được hình thành bởi sự đa dạng và biệt lập về mặt địa lý của khu vực. (Ảnh: Zhihu).
Ross Anderson thuộc Cơ quan Công viên Quốc gia và Động vật hoang dã cho biết: "Loài này được cho là đã tuyệt chủng ở Nam Úc và không có ghi chép chính thức nào trong khoảng hơn 100 năm. Tất nhiên, đã có một số trường hợp nhìn thấy không chính thức, nhưng không có chứng cứ để xác minh. Và thật ngạc nhiên khi hiện tại loài động vật được cho là đã tuyệt chủng lại đột nhiên xuất hiện".
Anderson cho biết: "Nó từng được cho là đã tuyệt chủng ở đây do mất môi trường sống và cạnh tranh với các loài động vật như mèo và cáo. Cho đến ngày nay, chúng tôi vẫn không chắc còn bao nhiêu cá thể bên ngoài tự nhiên trên toàn luc địa Úc".
Mèo túi đuôi đốm thường được chia thành hai loại. Mèo túi phương Tây có miếng đệm dạng hạt và năm ngón chân ở bàn chân sau. Chúng rất thích hợp để tồn tại vào ban đêm vì đôi mắt to và đôi tai sắc bén. Đuôi của chúng có một vệt màu đen chạy dọc đến ngọn. Mèo túi phương Đông trước đây đã lan rộng khắp nước Úc từ hàng triệu năm trước. Trên lục địa Úc, loài mèo túi phương Đông cuối cùng được cho là đã chết vào năm 1963. (Ảnh: A-z-animals)
Dasyurus là tên khoa học của toàn bộ chi mèo túi. Được dịch từ tiếng Latin, cái tên này có nghĩa là "đuôi lông", phản ánh đặc điểm nổi bật nhất của loài động vật này. Mèo túi có quan hệ gần gũi với quỷ Tasmania, dunnart và một số loài thú có túi nhỏ khác. Dựa trên phân tích di truyền, các nhà khoa học kết luận rằng những con mèo túi đầu tiên đã tiến hóa vào khoảng 15 triệu năm trước và sáu loài còn sống đều có thể truy tìm nguồn gốc của chúng từ một tổ tiên chung khoảng bốn triệu năm trước. Một số loài đã tuyệt chủng đã được xác định từ hồ sơ hóa thạch. (Ảnh: A-z-animals).
Mèo túi là loài thú có túi ăn thịt. Nó có thể được phân biệt bằng mõm dài, mũi hồng, đuôi có lông, tai to, răng sắc nhọn, thân dài và có màu lông màu nâu hoặc đen có đốm trắng. Đặc điểm nổi bật của thú có túi là cái túi bụng lớn dùng để mang và bảo vệ con non chưa phát triển. (Ảnh: CNN).
Một điểm đặc biệt của mèo túi là con đực sẽ chết hàng loạt sau khi giao phối, con cái sẽ nuôi con một mình, chúng sẽ bảo vệ con mình trong cái túi trước bụng. (Ảnh: ZME).
Mèo túi phải đối mặt với vô số mối đe dọa nguy hiểm trong tự nhiên. Khi được du nhập vào Úc, các loài động vật không phải bản địa như cáo và mèo đã gây bất ổn cho quần thể mèo túi. Chúng không chỉ săn mèo túi mà còn cạnh tranh với chúng để giành thức ăn và tài nguyên. Các nguồn nguy hiểm tiềm tàng khác bao gồm trăn, chó dingos, đại bàng và cú. (Ảnh: Zhihu).
Sự du nhập của loài cóc mía độc tới Úc vào năm 1935 cũng có tác động tàn khốc đến quần thể mèo túi địa phương. Ban đầu cóc mía được đưa đến Úc từ châu Mỹ, cóc mía được coi là có hiệu quả trong việc kiểm soát sâu bệnh, nhưng thay vào đó, nó lại có tác dụng ngoài ý muốn là đầu độc và giết chết các loài động vật ăn thịt bản địa của Úc. Loài cóc vẫn còn tồn tại ở phần lớn vùng đông bắc Australia và loài mèo túi dường như không có sức đề kháng hoặc khả năng miễn dịch tự nhiên với chất độc đến từ loài cóc mía. (Ảnh: CNN).
Mùa sinh sản của mèo túi bắt đầu vào mùa thu hoặc mùa đông ở Úc từ tháng 4 đến tháng 7. Mèo túi có thời gian mang thai khoảng ba tuần. Một số cá thể đặc biệt có thể sinh tới 30 con cùng một lúc, nhưng chỉ có 6 đến 8 con non có khả năng sống sót vì đó là số lượng tối đa mà mèo túi mẹ có thể cho con bú cùng một lúc. Tuổi thọ thông thường của loài này là từ hai đến năm năm, tuy nhiên rất ít cá thể đực có thể sống sau mùa giao phối đầu tiên hoặc thứ hai. Tuổi thọ tối đa từng được ghi nhận trong điều kiện nuôi nhốt là khoảng bảy năm. (Ảnh: A-z-animals).

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 2, 2000: Expedition 1 Arrives at the International Space Station
articles.text:
On this day in space! Nov. 2, 2000: Expedition 1 Arrives at the International Space Station
On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents.
On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. The mission was called Expedition 1.
Before this expedition, NASA had launched five, one-week-long Space Shuttle missions to help build the space station and bring up supplies. But this time, the crew would be staying for four and a half months, and they weren't taking the shuttle. Instead, they took a Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and this was the first Soyuz to ever dock at the space station.
During their stay at the space station, they unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the first solar arrays. They left on the space shuttle Discovery, which brought up the Expedition 2 crew that would take their place.
Why it mattered
As of today, there has been a continuous astronaut presence in space aboard the International Space Station for 26 years. For all of these years, not a day has gone by without someone living in space, orbiting our planet from aboard the space station.
While the ISS was not the first space station, it has been the longest-running space statin by far. This first crew were pioneers, showing how humans could actually live and work aboard this station. This exploratory mission proved that the station could successfully support astronaut crews.
Since this mission 26 years ago, there have been literally hundreds of astronauts from around the world who have flown to and lived aboard the ISS. While NASA has stated that the station might be decommissioned in the coming years, these accomplishments will remain forever in spaceflight history.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.
- Chelsea Gohd Content Manager

articles.title: NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover breaks historic record after traveling 28 miles
articles.text:
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover breaks historic record after traveling 28 miles
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a historic record by traveling 28.10 miles across Mars, farther than any vehicle has ever driven on another world. Armed with groundbreaking autonomous navigation technology and increasingly advanced driving capabilities, the rover is pushing the boundaries of robotic exploration.
- Share:
NASA's Perseverance rover has reached an impressive new milestone, traveling farther across another world than any vehicle before it. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), the rover's total driving distance reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), establishing a new record for travel on another celestial body. The achievement was even recognized by Guinness World Records, which presented a commemorative plaque to Perseverance's engineering twin on Earth.
The rover had actually come close to breaking the record about two months earlier. On Sol 1947, Perseverance was just 200 meters short of the milestone, a distance it could have covered in a single trip using its Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav) system.
But reaching the record was not the team's immediate priority. Perseverance was exploring an area filled with scientifically valuable ancient rock formations, so it spent weeks making short trips between locations to examine exposed rock surfaces. These investigations included grinding away thin layers of rock and conducting detailed measurements up close. Once the scientific work was complete, the rover resumed its journey and soon surpassed the previous distance record.
"Two months ago, (Perseverance) sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive... However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time (investigating) ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record."
How NASA Improved Perseverance's Driving Capabilities
Covering more than 28 miles on Mars has required Perseverance to overcome difficult terrain while testing new approaches to robotic driving. Its journeys through tightly packed boulder fields and across steep hillsides have given NASA engineers valuable experience, helping them improve the rover's ability to navigate hazardous landscapes.
To expand what Perseverance can safely handle, engineers conducted thousands of computer simulations and adjusted several operating limits. The rover can now tolerate tilts of up to 24 degrees, while the minimum clearance beneath its protective belly pan has been reduced to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches).
The team also introduced several important improvements to the driving system. Updated braking software helps the rover avoid collisions with rocks, and the electrical current limits for its steering motors have been nearly doubled. Engineers also added "dynamic slip tables" to its flight software, allowing the rover to better anticipate how much its wheels might slip on different surfaces.
Another technique involves driving across slopes in ways that help keep the wheels securely positioned on exposed bedrock. Together, these changes allow Perseverance to handle challenging terrain more effectively as it continues exploring Mars.
A Mars Rover That Can Navigate Without GPS
Among the rover's most significant technological advances is a system called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). This technology gives Perseverance a way to determine its position on Mars without relying on directions from Earth.
The system uses a powerful commercial processor originally installed in the Ingenuity Helicopter Base Station. By comparing images captured from the Martian surface with pictures taken from orbit, it can calculate the rover's location in global coordinates after completing a drive (as though we had GPS on a world without it).
Knowing its position independently is a major advantage. It allows Perseverance to cover greater distances without needing people on Earth to repeatedly determine its location, potentially making future exploration faster and more efficient.
However, this approach introduced an engineering challenge. Unlike the rover's main flight computer, the additional processor was not specifically designed to withstand the intense radiation conditions on Mars. The planet has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, leaving electronics exposed to radiation that can interfere with their operation.
In particular, radiation can cause "transient bit flips" that unexpectedly change information stored in computer memory, potentially disrupting software. To address this problem, engineers developed software protections that help the processor operate reliably despite the harsh environment.
The Next Frontier in Autonomous Mars Exploration
NASA is also investigating how generative AI could make the rover even more independent. As missions involve longer journeys and increasingly complex operations, the team wants to reduce the time and resources needed to plan safe routes.
The technology could help generate driving plans for the many individual segments of a longer journey, providing guidance that Perseverance's AutoNav system can use to navigate the terrain.
After traveling 45 kilometers (more than 28 miles), Perseverance has already provided engineers with extensive experience in navigating the Martian landscape. Those lessons are now shaping new technologies that could transform how robotic explorers operate on distant worlds.
And the journey is far from over. As Perseverance continues climbing higher along the rim of its Martian crater, NASA is preparing for the next major advances in autonomous exploration.
Story Source:

articles.title: Ancient blood found in 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil, study claims
articles.text:
Traces of ancient blood found in 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil, new study claims
Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.
Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.
However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.
In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.
The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.
"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."
Deep in the bones
The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?
To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.
"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."
The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.
A time capsule
Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats — thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.
"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."
The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.
Not everyone is convinced
While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.
"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."
For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.
According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.
Related stories
- Rare armored dinosaur found in Japan may have ancestors that migrated across a land bridge 100 million years ago
- Fossil of 'unconquered female warrior' dinosaur with long claws found in UK museum drawer after 100 years
- Remarkably preserved feathered dinosaur discovered in China reveals new secrets of flying-predator evolution
"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

articles.title: A rainbow of ancient rocks on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 2, 2026
articles.text:
A rainbow of ancient rocks on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 2, 2026
Turns out rainbow road is on Mars.
This rainbow-hued rocky plain looks like the landscape of an alien world. And, it turns out, it is.
What is it?
In this image, we can see an ancient, rocky hill on Mars. In the Red Planet's Southern Highlands, this alien terrain is chock-full of minerals, which we can see clearly defined in this color-enhanced view of the region.
This image was snapped by the HiRISE camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), which has been studying the planet's surface, atmosphere and climate since arriving in Martian orbit in March 2006.
But this isn't exactly what the surface of the planet would look like through our eyes; the image is color-enhanced. Why would scientists take a natural-color image and turn it rainbow? Doing so enhances the slight color differences in these rocks, allowing researchers to pick out the different minerals.
Why is it incredible?
As pointed to above, enhancing colors in scientific images can be an incredibly useful tool for exploration.
For instance, in this image, the blue- and green-toned rocks could be full of minerals like pyroxenes and olivine, according to scientists analyzing the image. And they think that the yellow, orange and red patches may contain minerals formed by past interactions with liquid water.
By exploring the mineral content of rocks like this, researchers can peel back the layers of history within the Martian bedrock. The discovery of certain minerals, for example, can show that water flowed on Mars long ago, pointing to potentially habitable conditions.
So, as we can see, this striking rainbow image isn't just a beautiful landscape; it's also hiding serious clues to Mars' history.
Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. articles.title: Điều xảy ra khi thời gian ngừng lại?
articles.text:
Khái niệm ngưng đọng thời gian xuất hiện trên phim ảnh khá nhiều. Tuy vậy, việc ngưng đọng thời gian dưới góc nhìn khoa học không lãng mạn như trên phim.
Nếu cảm thấy chưa đủ thời gian cho một ngày, có bao giờ bạn tự hỏi nếu mình có năng lực như Dr. Strange, ngưng đọng thời gian thì mọi chuyện sẽ như thế nào không?
Trong các bộ phim khoa học viễn tưởng, việc một người ngưng đọng được thời gian được diễn tả theo cách người đó sẽ tiếp tục sinh hoạt trong khi mọi người khác đứng im.
Ngưng đọng thời gian là khái niệm xuất hiện nhiều trên phim ảnh.
Nhưng theo các định luật khoa học, việc ngưng đọng thời gian không lãng mạn như vậy.
Để trả lời câu hỏi trên, bận cần biết thực chất thời gian là gì?
Đó có thể là những cây kim dịch chuyển trên mặt đồng hồ. Cũng có thể nó là những con số hiển thị trên màn hình điện thoại hay cách mặt trời mọc rồi lặn và sinh nhật bạn tổ chức hàng năm. Đó là tất cả những điều thân thuộc khi mọi người nghĩ đến thời gian.
Nhưng nếu đi vào thuật ngữ khoa học, thời gian là sự tiến triển của các hoạt động từ quá khứ đến hiện tại và tương lai. Những nhà vật lý có thể định nghĩa thời gian phức tạp hơn. Nhưng xét cho cùng nó cũng chỉ là hệ thống đo lường.
Theo công thức tính vận tốc thì vận tốc sẽ bằng khoảng cách chia cho thời gian. Như vậy nếu thời gian ngưng đọng, biến số thời gian sẽ là 0. Bạn không thể chia một số cho 0.
Như vậy, nếu không có thời gian sẽ không có khoảng cách, không có vận tốc. Nói cách khác, nếu dừng thời gian thì mọi thứ sẽ không thể chuyển động.
Điều này đồng nghĩa sẽ không có ánh sáng vì hạt photon, đơn vị cơ bản của ánh sáng, vật nhanh nhất trong vũ trụ không thể di chuyển. Hạt photon không chuyển động và đi vào mắt vì vậy bạn sẽ không thể nhìn thấy gì.
Không khí cũng không thể di chuyển vì vậy con người sẽ không thể hít thở. Máu cũng sẽ không cần Oxy bởi nó không còn lưu thông nữa. Với sự ngưng đọng của phân tử, nhiệt độ cũng chẳng còn, dẫn đến trời sẽ rất lạnh.
Như vậy, nếu không có thời gian, con người sẽ bị nghẹt thở, mù và đông cứng.
Trong khi đó, bên ngoài Trái đất, các lực cơ bản của vũ trụ cũng sẽ dừng hẳn. Theo thuyết tương đối của Einstein, không gian và thời gian được kết nối theo công thức E=mc^2.
Vì vậy, không có thời gian, không gian sẽ không thể tồn tại. Nếu dừng thời gian đồng nghĩa với dừng mọi thứ mà con người đang biết. Không có vũ trụ và không có gì cả.
Nguyên bản ngưng đọng thời gian của một bộ phim khoa học viễn tưởng chỉ có thể sẽ ra nếu nó giữ lại các định luật vật lý.
“Đóng băng thời gian” bằng ảo giác chronostasis
Nếu bóc tách vấn đề ra khỏi phạm vi vật lý, thời gian không chỉ là thứ được đọc trên đồng hồ. Đó cũng là cảm giác mà chúng ta có trong đầu và cơ thể. Nó là một nhịp điệu tự nhiên của thế giới. Thời gian có thể có lúc cảm giác rất nhanh, có lúc lại cảm giác trôi rất chậm.
Craig Callender cho biết ấn tượng chủ quan của mỗi người về thời gian sẽ khiến câu hỏi “Thời gian có dừng được không?” đi theo một hướng thú vị khác hẳn.
Có một ảo ảnh tâm lý nổi tiếng được gọi là "chronostasis". Bạn có thể tự thực hiện thí nghiệm để trải nghiệm cảm giác chronostasis tạo ra. Hãy đặt một chiếc đồng hồ ở rìa tầm nhìn của mình, sau đó nhìn chằm chằm vào thứ khác trong giây lát. Khi liếc lại chiếc đồng hồ và tập trung vào kim giây, bạn sẽ thấy kim giây bất động, thời gian tưởng chừng như vừa dừng lại.
Ảo ảnh này xuất hiện liên quan đến chuyển động của mắt gọi là saccades. Khi nhãn cầu của bạn nhấp nháy qua lại rất nhanh để liên tục tiếp nhận hình ảnh môi trường xung quanh, để ngăn bạn nhìn thấy một vùng mờ hỗn loạn, bộ não của ta sẽ tự động chỉnh sửa những gì nó nhìn thấy trong thời gian thực và tạo ra ấn tượng về một trường nhìn liên tục.
“Nếu chúng ta chỉ bàn về cảm giác chủ quan của mình về thời gian, thì chúng ta có thể “đóng băng” nó một lúc bằng cách tạo ra ảo ảnh chronostasis cho chính mình. Đây đã là điều gần nhất mà con người có thể làm được lúc này rồi”, Callender nói.

articles.title: NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice
articles.text:
NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- NASA satellites have captured an eerie, skull-shaped formation on a remote Antarctic island, but its haunting appearance conceals a troubling warning about melting glaciers. Unusually warm winter temperatures have exposed large areas of dark ice, potentially accelerating future melting and gradually transforming the skull's ghostly features.
- Share:
Located in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, Vega Island has a particularly haunting appearance when viewed from above. Its rocky and icy features resemble a grinning skull seen from the side, seemingly gazing toward nearby Devil Island. But behind this unusual sight is a more serious story about the changing condition of Antarctica's glaciers.
NASA Satellite Images Reveal Antarctica's Icy Skull
NASA satellite images show the island during the beginning of Antarctic autumn and during spring. The images were captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.)
Several natural landmarks create the skull's distinctive appearance. A nunatak, which is a rocky peak rising above the surrounding ice, resembles an empty eye socket. A lateral moraine, a ridge of material left along the side of a glacier, outlines the mouth. Meanwhile, Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier forms what looks like the skull's lower jaw.
The two satellite views also reveal a striking difference in snow coverage. In March 2025, snow blanketed the icy terrain, consistent with March being the wettest month in the region. By October 2026, however, extensive sections of the island were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.
Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College explained that unusually warm conditions during the winter of 2026, especially in June, contributed to the unusually large areas of exposed ice observed in October. According to Pelto, the exposed surfaces on Vega Island and neighboring islands suggest that relatively little fresh snow accumulated over the winter. Some of that snow was also lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and through strong winds that swept snow away.
“The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”
Why Exposed Ice Could Accelerate Glacier Melting
The lack of snow could have important consequences as Antarctica moves into its warmer months. Fresh snow reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it, while darker, exposed ice absorbs more solar energy. As daylight increases and temperatures rise, these darker surfaces are likely to warm more quickly, potentially speeding up glacier melting.
Even a modest amount of new snowfall could temporarily slow that process by covering the exposed ice.
“Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said.
Continued melting could also gradually transform the island's unsettling appearance. The same ice and rock formations that give Vega Island its skull shape are vulnerable to changes as the glaciers retreat.
“When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”
Decades of Glacier Loss on Vega Island
Scientists have been studying Vega Island's glaciers for decades, and satellite observations have played an important role in documenting their condition.
One of the earliest detailed surveys appeared in a 1982 study that used early Landsat satellite data, aerial photography, and topographic maps to examine the island's ice cover. Researchers identified four ice caps, along with rocky cliffs extending above the ice and glaciers flowing outward from the ice caps. Altogether, they documented 29 glaciers across Vega Island.
One of these, Devil's Bay Glacier, has been monitored in detail since the Antarctic summer of 1998-1999. Measurements collected over that period show an overall reduction in the glacier's mass.
The changes are not limited to Devil's Bay Glacier. Satellite observations spanning recent decades reveal that other glaciers on Vega Island have also lost ice, exposing increasing amounts of the underlying bedrock.
Vega Island's Remarkable Antarctic Survival Story
Long before satellites began monitoring its ice, Vega Island played an unexpected role in one of Antarctica's dramatic early exploration stories.
The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 traveled to the region to investigate the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding areas. What began as a scientific mission turned into a desperate struggle for survival.
During the expedition, the explorers became separated into three groups, each forced to endure the Antarctic winter in a different location. Their situation became even more dangerous when pack ice destroyed their ship, leaving them stranded in one of the world's most unforgiving environments.
Despite the ordeal, Vega Island eventually became the setting for a moment of hope. In spring 1903, two of the separated groups reunited at a location later named Cape Well-met, near what now resembles the “forehead” of the island's giant skull.
Not long afterward, an Argentinean expedition arrived and rescued the survivors, bringing their extraordinary Antarctic ordeal to an end.
Today, Vega Island remains a place where dramatic natural formations, a remarkable history of exploration, and the effects of a changing climate come together. Its ghostly skull may be one of Antarctica's most unusual sights, but the gradual transformation of the ice that shapes it tells an even more important story.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

articles.title: 'VisionQuest' homework guide: Everything you need to watch to understand Marvel's WandaVision follow-up
articles.text:
'VisionQuest' homework guide: Everything you need to watch to understand Marvel's WandaVision follow-up
Marvel Studios' existential superhero series "VisionQuest" has arrived on Disney+, and we've already been treated to four intriguing episodes that delve into the complex life of Vision, Paul Bettany's intelligent android and former card-carrying member of The Avengers.
The staggered storyline leading up to this show began with 2021's "WandaVision" and the 2024 follow-up, "Agatha All Along," with Marvel Studios proclaiming "VisionQuest" to be "the final vision of the groundbreaking trilogy." So, for those trying to catch up on current events in this trilogy of MCU shows starring Vision, and to avoid any lingering confusion, let’s take a step back to fill in the gaps.
And now, this isn't as simple as just "watch all the Marvel movies and shows in order," because that is a frankly ridiculous undertaking and entirely too much homework to do before watching a show. We're distilling it down to just what you need to know to understand VisionQuest.
Spoiler warning: It should go without saying, but there are spoilers for previous Marvel movies and shows in this article. You have been warned!
TLDR: Marvel shows and movies you need to watch ahead of VisionQuest
We'll go into some detail on all the connections below, but if you just want a list of the essential Marvel shows and movies to watch before VisionQuest, here it is.
Note that this is just the essentials. There are loads of small references to other movies and shows in the MCU, but they're just nods.
- Avengers: Age of Ultron
- Avengers: Infinity War
- WandaVision
- Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness*
- Agatha All Along
*This one is debatable. It continues Wanda's story from WandaVision, but it's not really essential for understanding the events of VisionQuest.
Both are the true vision. Neither is the true Vision
We kick things off with 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War," where the mighty Thanos murdered Vision by plucking out his golden, forehead-mounted Mind Stone for his Infinity Gauntlet. From that moment forward, Vision was dead, and Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) was cast into unfathomable grief and not-so-repressed anger.
From there, we pick up the story in the 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision." Set weeks after "Avengers: Endgame," this show features two separate versions of Vision.
One was a new synthezoid version, Frankensteined together from the components of the old Vision by S.W.O.R.D., nicknamed White Vision. The other Vision is a supernatural manifestation, brought to life via Wanda Maximoff’s sorcery; he is known as Hex Vision.
So, which of these two Visions appears in "VisionQuest"? That's the fun (and confusing) part, because the answer is both of them. At the end of "WandaVision," Hex Vision restores the lost memories of White Vision, essentially merging two entities into one.
So, the Vision we see in "VisionQuest" is the physical body of White Vision, injected with thoughts and remembrances of the model that was magically resurrected by Wanda. Confused yet? Don't worry, it's going to get weirder.
Voices inside my head
In addition to the two versions of Vision from "WandaVision," numerous other AIs exist within Vision's skull and are all represented by human avatars acting as factions of his ravaged psyche.
Cast your mind all the way back to 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and you'll remember that Vision was conceived from a combination of the artificial brain of Ultron, the Mind Stone, and fragments of Tony Stark’s AI butler companion, J.A.R.V.I.S., who was named after the real Jarvis seen in the "Agent Carter" TV series.
J.A.R.V.I.S. appears in "VisionQuest" as his own unique entity, alongside another of Tony Stark's AI helpers, E.D.I.T.H., aka the AI in the smart glasses that Stark left to Peter Parker after his death. She shows up in "Spider-Man: Far From Home," which is a great movie but not an essential viewing if you're preparing for "VisionQuest."
Then let's toss in the fact that papa Ultron (James Spader) is buzzing around in Vision’s cranium, creating what’s been described as more or less an "Age of Ultron" and a "WandaVision" sequel at the same time. As it turns out, Vision did not destroy Ultron at the end of "Age of Ultron"; he copied his code and absorbed him, so now the rabid robot lives on in Vision’s brain.
Like father, like son
The show’s narrative is centered around the complicated relationship between Vision and his son Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). Tommy was created by Wanda's Hex and should have disappeared when it collapsed, but both he and his brother Billy survived through magical shenanigans that are explained in 2024's "Agatha All Along."
Those two Maximoff boys, Tommy and Billy, both vanished from existence at the conclusion of "WandaVision." "Agatha All Along" exposed the truth that their consciousnesses entered the ether before expiring, only to reemerge into the souls of two teenage boys who had just perished, therefore returning them to life. Are you still with us? Good, just checking.
The finale of "Agatha All Along" hinted at the return of the estranged Tommy, and "VisionQuest" dives into that dangling plot point with relish!
Palad-in for a bad time
Every show needs an antagonist, and the voices in Vision's head can't do all the work. "VisionQuest" has introduced a duo of villains for Vision to contend with. Neither of them has shown up in the MCU previously, though, so you don't need to do any research here.
With a massive bounty on his head after breaking free from S.W.O.R.D.'s control, White Vision must contend with a new villainous foe in the form of a mysterious mercenary named Paladin (Todd Stashwick).
This enigmatic Marvel Comics character was created by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino and was first seen prowling the pages of "Daredevil #150" back in 1978. He's basically a gun-for-hire in the Marvel universe, often hired to fight alongside or against various heroes depending on the story. We don't know much about his motivations in the show, but we'll learn more as it goes on.
"VisionQuest" also shines a spotlight on the bizarro character of Ultron's "bride," Jocasta, though the MCU version of this character diverges wildly from the comic book inspiration.
It's enough to drive one to madness! Between all the father-son dynamics dancing around the eight scheduled episodes, being hunted down by mercs, and his transcendent search for meaning, Vision and his saga are hopefully headed to a peaceful end.
Created by Terry Matalas ("Star Trek: Picard," "12 Monkeys") and airing two new chapters each Tuesday night on Disney+, VisionQuest is bolstered by a cast that includes Ruaridh Mollica, T'Nia Miller, Lauren Morais, Orla Brady, Diane Morgan, Polly Frame, Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, Emily Hampshire, and James D’Arcy.

His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.
