articles.title: Mysterious 2,600-year-old Egyptian building discovered from space — and it could be an ancient tomb or shrine
articles.text:
Buried for 2,600 years beneath Nile mud, a massive ancient Egyptian complex was just found — from space
Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.
Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.
The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.
Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.
Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.
First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).
To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.
The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.
And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.
That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.
The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.
"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."
The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.
A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.
Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.
A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.
Related stories
The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.
"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."
The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

Wafaa Tantawy is an Egyptian archaeologist and heritage conservation specialist who graduated from Cairo University. She specializes in archaeological conservation and ancient Egyptian material culture, and brings firsthand field experience from Egyptian archaeological sites. Her work has been published on Ancient Origins and Medium, where she focuses on making Egypt's rich archaeological record accessible to global audiences.

articles.title: Tàu đổ bộ Ấn Độ gửi hình ảnh Mặt trăng đẹp choáng ngợp khi chuẩn bị hạ cánh
articles.text:
Tàu vũ trụ Chandrayaan-3 của Ấn Độ đang lao vun vút gần Mặt trăng trước nỗ lực hạ cánh lịch sử và nó đã ghi lại một số hình ảnh tuyệt đẹp trên đường đi.
Tổ chức Nghiên cứu Vũ trụ Ấn Độ (ISRO) ngày 22/8 đã xác nhận rằng tàu vũ trụ Chandrayaan-3 đang theo đúng lịch trình và hoạt động của tàu tiếp tục "thuận buồm xuôi gió”. Tàu đổ bộ Vikram của sứ mạng Chandrayaan-3 dự kiến sẽ bắt đầu hạ cánh xuống bề mặt Mặt trăng vào 17h45 ngày 23/8 theo giờ Ấn Độ (tức 19h15 cùng ngày theo giờ Việt Nam).
Camera Lander Imager 4 của tàu vũ trụ Chandrayaan-3 chụp được hình ảnh cận cảnh bề mặt Mặt trăng vào ngày 20/8.
Nếu thành công, sứ mệnh này sẽ đánh dấu lần hạ cánh mềm đầu tiên trên bề mặt Mặt trăng của tàu vũ trụ Ấn Độ và đưa nước này trở thành quốc gia thứ tư trên thế giới từng đạt được kỳ tích như vậy. Hiện nay, Mỹ, Trung Quốc và Liên Xô cũ là những quốc gia đã tiến hành thành công hạ cánh có kiểm soát tàu vũ trụ lên Mặt trăng.
Cơ quan vũ trụ của Ấn Độ sẽ phát trực tiếp nỗ lực hạ cánh của Chandrayaan-3 bắt đầu lúc 17h20 giờ chuẩn Ấn Độ ngày 23/8.
Tổ chức Nghiên cứu Vũ trụ Ấn Độ ngày 21/8 đã đánh dấu đêm trước sự kiện sứ mạng Chandrayaan-3 hạ cánh bằng cách chia sẻ ảnh và cảnh quay được ghi lại bằng camera trên tàu vũ trụ này.
Một hình ảnh rõ nét về bề mặt Mặt trăng được chụp từ độ cao 70 km, đã mô tả các đặc điểm như Mare Marginis, một vết đen lớn được hình thành do các tiểu hành tinh cổ đại va vào rìa cực "mặt gần" của Mặt trăng ("The near side" là bán cầu Mặt trăng luôn hướng về Trái đất, ngược lại với "mặt xa" - far side. Chỉ có thể nhìn thấy một mặt của Mặt trăng từ Trái đất vì Mặt trăng quay trên trục của nó với cùng tốc độ mà Mặt trăng quay quanh Trái đất).
Một hình ảnh khác, được chụp vào ngày 20/8 từ một vị trí thuận lợi gần hơn nhiều khi tàu vũ trụ lướt qua, cung cấp cận cảnh về địa hình xám xịt bụi bặm của Mặt trăng.
Theo cơ quan vũ trụ Ấn Độ, tàu Chandrayaan-3 có thể định hướng vị trí của nó bằng cách khớp các hình ảnh do camera chụp được với bản đồ Mặt trăng được lập trình trong máy tính trên tàu.
Tàu Chandrayaan, có nghĩa là "phương tiện Mặt trăng" trong tiếng Phạn, được phóng từ Trung tâm vũ trụ Satish Dhawan tại Sriharikota, bang Andhra Pradesh miền nam Ấn Độ vào ngày 14/7. Tàu vũ trụ này đã thực hiện một cách tiếp cận chậm rãi đối với bề mặt Mặt trăng.
Cơ quan vũ trụ của Ấn Độ ISRO công bố hình ảnh về khu vực "mặt xa" của Mặt trăng được chụp bởi Camera Lander Imager 4 trên tàu Chandrayaan-3. Tàu đổ bộ của Ấn Độ đang chuẩn bị hạ cánh mềm xuống vùng cực nam của Mặt trăng.
Sứ mệnh Chandrayaan-3 đánh dấu nỗ lực thứ hai của Ấn Độ nhằm hoàn thành cuộc đổ bộ có kiểm soát lên Mặt trăng. Nỗ lực đầu tiên, vào năm 2019 với Chandrayaan-2, đã chứng kiến tàu đổ bộ đâm xuống bề mặt Mặt trăng do sự cố phần mềm và khó phanh khi hạ cánh.
Trạm đổ bộ Vikram trên tàu vũ trụ Chandrayaan-3 mang theo một robot nhỏ gọi là Pragyan. Bộ đôi chạy bằng năng lượng Mặt Trời này sẽ khám phá bề mặt trong một ngày Mặt trăng (bằng khoảng 14 ngày Trái đất), trước khi đêm Mặt trăng (cũng dài bằng 14 ngày Trái đất) tối và lạnh buông xuống, khiến chúng cạn kiệt pin.
Vikram đã tới gần Mặt trăng hơn hôm 20/8, sau khi hoàn thành thao tác de-boosting (giảm tốc để điều chỉnh vị trí trên quỹ đạo) cuối cùng. Với thao tác này, trạm đổ bộ đã tới quỹ đạo mà điểm gần Mặt trăng nhất là 25km và xa nhất là 134km. ISRO cho biết, nó sẽ trải qua quá trình tự kiểm tra và chờ thời điểm Mặt trời mọc tại địa điểm hạ cánh chỉ định.
Trạm đổ bộ này nhắm đến điểm hạ cánh gần cực nam Mặt trăng, nơi có khả năng cao tồn tại băng nước hữu ích cho việc chế tạo nhiên liệu đẩy hoặc duy trì sự sống.
Vikram mang 4 bộ thiết bị khoa học, trong đó có đầu dò nhiệt với khả năng đâm sâu vào đất Mặt trăng khoảng 10cm và ghi nhận nhiệt độ của đất đá xuyên suốt ngày Mặt trăng. Vikram cũng trang bị một bộ phản xạ ngược, dự kiến vẫn phát huy tác dụng rất lâu sau khi trạm đổ bộ này ngừng hoạt động. Trong khi đó, robot Pragyan mang theo Máy quang phổ phát xạ laser (LIBS) và Máy quang phổ tia X hạt Alpha (APXS) để nghiên cứu đất đá Mặt trăng.
Chỉ ít ngày trước thời điểm Chandrayaan-3 dự kiến hạ cánh, sứ mạng Luna-25 của Nga đã gặp sự cố, khiến tàu đổ bộ này rơi xuống bề mặt Mặt trăng.
Ngày 21/8, người đứng đầu cơ quan vũ trụ Roscosmos của Nga, Yury Borisov, đã tiết lộ nguyên nhân chính dẫn đến thất bại của sứ mạng Luna-25 là do tàu thăm dò đã không tắt động cơ kịp thời và đi chệch khỏi quỹ đạo dự kiến.
“Thật không may, việc tắt động cơ không diễn ra bình thường, theo sơ đồ trình tự, mà dựa trên dấu thời gian (time stamp), và thay vì 84 giây theo kế hoạch, nó đã diễn ra trong 127 giây", ông Borisov nói với đài truyền hình Rossiya 24. Yếu tố này là nguyên nhân quan trọng đằng sau sự thất bại của sứ mạng - ông Borisov tuyên bố và cho biết thêm rằng một ủy ban đặc biệt đã được thành lập để điều tra vụ việc.

articles.title: 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought
articles.text:
30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought
Europeans were traveling, mixing, and maintaining surprisingly far-reaching connections more than 30,000 years ago.
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- University of Vienna
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered surprising DNA evidence that Europeans living more than 30,000 years ago were connected across vast distances, challenging the idea that ancient populations remained largely isolated. Genetic clues from human remains and cave sediments reveal prehistoric migration, long-lasting communities, and survival through the harshest conditions of the Ice Age.
- Share:
More than 30,000 years ago, people living across Ice Age Europe were far more connected than scientists previously believed. New genetic evidence reveals unexpected links between populations separated by enormous distances, challenging the long-held idea that eastern and western European groups remained largely isolated from one another.
An international research team led by the University of Vienna made the discovery by analyzing ancient DNA from rare human remains and traces of human genetic material preserved in cave sediments. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide a new picture of how prehistoric Europeans interacted, exchanged genes, and maintained populations through thousands of years of dramatic environmental change.
The research focuses on people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian), which flourished across the continent roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. Archaeological discoveries have long suggested that these ancient populations maintained connections over considerable distances. However, previous genetic evidence pointed to relatively distinct eastern and western ancestry groups.
By combining new genetic findings with previously collected DNA, researchers uncovered evidence that these groups were more interconnected than expected. They also found signs that certain populations in southwestern Europe maintained their genetic ancestry for thousands of years.
A Woman From 30,000 Years Ago Reveals Hidden Genetic Connections
One of the most revealing discoveries came from the remains of a woman who lived approximately 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France. Found at Isturitz Cave, her remains provided the oldest genome-wide genetic dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe.
Her DNA contained a surprising combination of ancestry. Although most of her genetic background was associated with western European populations, she also carried ancestry linked to people from central and eastern Europe.
Using genetic modeling, researchers estimated that this mixing between populations occurred approximately 32,500 to 31,500 years ago. The finding suggests that genetic connections extended across large portions of Europe much earlier than scientists had previously established.
"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. "Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected."
The researchers identified a similar genetic signature in another ancient individual whose remains had previously been studied at Ormesson, France. Combined with archaeological discoveries, the evidence strengthens the possibility that Isturitz Cave served as a gathering place where different groups of prehistoric people encountered one another.
Ancient DNA Hidden in Cave Sediments Reveals Ice Age Survival
While some ancient Europeans exchanged genes across considerable distances, other populations appear to have maintained a continuous genetic presence in particular regions for thousands of years.
Evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain suggests that ancestry associated with western European populations persisted in southwestern Europe over an extended period.
The researchers also used an increasingly valuable technique that allows scientists to recover human DNA directly from cave sediments, even when no identifiable human remains are present. Tiny traces of genetic material left behind by ancient inhabitants can survive in soil and other deposits for thousands of years, providing information about people whose bones have never been found.
At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, Spain, the team recovered human nuclear DNA from a sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years. Despite finding no human bones or teeth in the layer, they obtained enough genetic information to determine the ancestry of the people who had occupied the site.
"Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing," says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. "This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site."
The results indicate that western European ancestry persisted in the region through the Last Glacial Maximum, a period when enormous ice sheets reached their greatest extent during the last Ice Age.
This supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula, which includes present-day Spain and Portugal, served as an important refuge for prehistoric humans during some of the coldest conditions of the Ice Age.
Ancient Mother and Son Offer Clues About Prehistoric Mating
Another revealing discovery came from southern Italy, where researchers examined the genetic remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus believed to be the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1.
Genetic analysis suggests that the child's father likely belonged to the same ancestral population as his mother. However, the parents were not closely related, offering evidence that mating patterns within these ancient communities may have helped limit inbreeding.
This finding adds another dimension to the emerging picture of prehistoric European societies. Even as some populations maintained relatively stable genetic ancestry within their home regions, they could also participate in broader networks of genetic exchange spanning considerable distances.
Together, the discoveries show that long-term regional continuity and widespread genetic connections were not mutually exclusive. Both helped shape the population history of Ice Age Europe.
Building on these results, Gelabert and his colleagues are now combining DNA recovered from ancient sediments with advanced proteomic techniques, which examine proteins for clues about past life. Their goal is to investigate the earliest expansions of modern humans across Europe, including how these populations interacted with carnivores in places where bones and other organic remains are scarce.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Vienna. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pere Gelabert, Susanna Sawyer, Vanessa Villalba-Mouco, Olivia Cheronet, Victoria Oberreiter, Diego Gárate, Christian Normand, Lawrence G. Straus, Manuel R. González Morales, Igor Gutiérrez-Zugasti, David Cuenca-Solana, Joëlle Darricau, Henry de Lumley, José-Miguel Tejero, Mareike Stahlschmidt, Thomas Higham, Maddalena Giannì, Laura G. van der Sluis, Carla Gómez-Montes, Miriam Ibáñez-Herranz, Michelle Hämmerle, Brina Zagorc, Florian Exler, Florian Brück, Stefan Franz, Fernanda Tenorio Cano, Kristin Stewardson, Lijun Qiu, Ana B. Marín-Arroyo, Michaela Lucci, Alessia Nava, Francesco Genchi, Donato Coppola, Chiara La Marca, Alfredo Coppa, David Reich, Ron Pinhasi. Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (43) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128

articles.title: 'Now you actually have a blood test': Psychiatry's bible, the DSM, is getting upgraded to include biological markers. A psychiatrist explains what that means for mental health.
articles.text:
'Now you actually have a blood test': Psychiatry's bible, the DSM, is getting upgraded to include biological markers. A psychiatrist explains what that means for mental health.
Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.
For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.
But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.
Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.
Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.
Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?
Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.
An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.
The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.
It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.
KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?
AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."
The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.
For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.
In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.
And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.
But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.
I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.
Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.
But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.
With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.
So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."
It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.
KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?
AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.
Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.
It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.
Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.
That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.
KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?
AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.
There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.
That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.
For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.
I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.
So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.
KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?
AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- Adversity shaped our evolution as a species. People raised in it may have underrecognized strengths because of it.
- Ancient 'alien-like' skulls have been found on every continent but Antarctica. Anthropologists are starting to figure out why.
- Could psilocybin treat brain injuries? Neuroscientist explains how psychedelics could fill a gap in head trauma care
Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.
It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.
It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.
This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.
Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

articles.title: What is Starshield? A look at SpaceX's military satellite network
articles.text:
What is Starshield? A look at SpaceX's military satellite network
Starshield has been in the news a fair bit recently.
SpaceX is building and operating two satellite networks at the moment, Starlink and Starshield. What’s the difference between the two, and who uses them?
For more than a week in October 2026, Ukrainian drone operators found their high-speed satellite links shut off. Officials in Kyiv said that terminals for SpaceX’s Starshield network stopped working at speeds of above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) from Oct. 14, hampering efforts to conduct defensive operations and intercept Russian drones. Full connectivity was restored on Oct. 24, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The arguments over who did what continue, but the affair highlighted how little is publicly understood about Starshield — what it is, how it relates to Starlink, and how it is operated.
What is Starlink?
Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial, mass-market satellite internet service. The company says it now has more than 11,000 Starlink broadband and mobile satellites in orbit, operating approximately 342 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth. This follows years of deployment using the company's Falcon 9 rocket..
The network serves consumers, enterprises and government customers across more than 160 countries. It is owned and operated by SpaceX. Anyone from a rural household to an airline can buy a terminal and a service plan.
Governments are also customers, with public agencies using Starlink for a range of purposes including connectivity, disaster response and national security, notably in the case of Ukraine in the wake of the invasion by Russia, which began in February 2022 and is ongoing.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is SpaceX’s network for serving national security customers. The company announced the program in December 2022, stating it would apply Starlink technology and SpaceX's launch capability to government needs, initially in three areas: Earth observation, communications and hosted payloads.
"They are using the same satellite buses," says Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. “They look the same, but they have a lot more kit on them that allows them to do more things. They provide similar broadband internet, but with more secure hardware and software and hardened systems.”
The company says it has won multi-billion-dollar, multiyear contracts from the U.S. military in 2026 for Starshield-related services.
Some Starshield satellites may also carry sensors for intelligence and surveillance. But much about Starshield is secretive, with its finances not revealed and launches often classified.
Starshield makeup
Starshield is made up of a range of different assets, including spy satellites, military data satellites, and secure communications for ground users.
The spy satellites are sent into orbit in launches for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), for a "proliferated architecture" of spy satellites, including electro-optical, radar and relay spacecraft. The NRO does not use the Starshield name, but said earlier this year that it had launched more than 200 satellites in recent years, many of which are for its proliferated architecture.
Then there is the Space Data Network Backbone. The U.S. Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion fixed-price contract to build the network, previously known as MILNET, using Starshield satellites. It is meant to move data quickly between missile-warning sensors and interceptors as part of the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense plan. A prototype is due by the end of 2027. A Space Force official has described MILNET as government-owned and operated by SpaceX as a contractor, under Space Force oversight.
Starshield provides encrypted connectivity for military users through terminals. These can be dedicated Starshield terminals, or Starlink terminals for Starshield services.
Crucially, the networks overlap. "Those Starshield satellites are physically separate from Starlink satellites, but the Starshield satellites can use the Starlink network if they need to," Bowen said. That interoperability is available to U.S. national security users, he added, "but not if you're a commercial user of Starlink."
Use restrictions differ, too. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said that Starlink's terms of service bar its use for offensive drone strikes, while decisions about Starshield use rest with the U.S. government.
Who controls Starshield is a question that entered the public consciousness in the wake of the Ukraine Starshield speed limit affair. The U.S. government is the customer, and also in some cases the owner, but SpaceX builds the satellites, operates the underlying Starlink network on which some Starshield services run and, in some arrangements, operates the Starshield satellites themselves. How this command is divided between the government and SpaceX is unclear.
Bowen compared it to the U.K.’s Skynet military satellite system, in which contractor Babcock operates the satellites. "The actual button punching is done by the contractors, but the military and government are in the room and are calling the shots,” he said.
That question matters, because it determines whether SpaceX can act on its own or only with government oversight and approval.
What’s next?
Starshield appears set to become more central to U.S. military space. The Space Data Network Backbone prototype is expected next year, while NRO launches will continue, according to contracts. With SpaceX now a public company, quarterly reports could provide more insight into the system. For now, however, much remains classified.
Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

articles.title: Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds
articles.text:
Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health
- Summary:
- A major new study challenges the idea that moderate drinking is safe, finding that even relatively small amounts of alcohol increase the risk of cancer, heart disease, and premature death. Researchers found no overall health benefits from drinking and warn that consuming more than one alcoholic beverage per day can significantly increase long-term health risks.
- Share:
A major new study suggests that even modest amounts of alcohol may carry serious health consequences. Researchers found that drinking levels many Americans consider moderate are associated with higher risks of premature death, disability, cancer, heart disease, and other long-term health problems.
Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research challenges the longstanding belief that moderate drinking is harmless or may even provide health benefits. The findings suggest that alcohol's risks begin at relatively low levels of consumption and increase as people drink more.
"This study provides the most comprehensive U.S. estimates to date of lifetime risks of alcohol-attributable mortality and morbidity, showing that even moderate levels of consumption increase the risk of premature death and disability," said study co-author Katherine M. Keyes, PhD, professor of Epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.
"No protective effect of drinking was observed even at low levels," added Keyes, whose research examines alcohol and other substance use across different stages of life.
"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," said lead study author Kevin Shield, PhD, an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."
Major Study Examines the Lifetime Health Risks of Alcohol
To better understand how drinking affects health over a lifetime, researchers from the United States and Canada conducted an extensive review of existing scientific evidence.
Medical experts evaluated more than 7,200 scientific articles examining diseases and injuries associated with alcohol consumption. They used this evidence to determine how drinking influences the risk of individual health conditions, then combined those findings with large national health data sets.
Using statistical models, the team estimated how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious illnesses or dying prematurely over a lifetime.
The analysis covered a wide range of health problems linked to alcohol, including cardiovascular disease, liver disease, injuries, and several forms of cancer. Among the cancers examined were those affecting the esophagus, mouth, and breast.
By considering these conditions together, the researchers were able to estimate alcohol's overall health burden rather than focusing on individual diseases.
Why Two Drinks a Day May Be Riskier Than You Think
One of the study's most important findings concerns drinking habits that many people would not consider excessive.
Consuming two alcoholic drinks per day, a level often viewed as socially moderate, was associated with a substantially higher risk of premature death attributable to alcohol.
The findings also provide more specific information than the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines, which recommend that Americans "limit alcoholic beverages" but do not identify a particular amount that can be consumed safely.
Earlier dietary recommendations set daily limits of two alcoholic drinks for men and one for women. However, what counts as a single drink depends on the beverage and its alcohol content. A standard drink generally corresponds to 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits, although differences in alcohol concentration can change those amounts.
According to the researchers, the newer guidelines communicate a useful 'less-is-best' principle but lack specific numerical estimates that would help people understand how health risks change with consumption.
Their analysis was intended to fill that gap by measuring risks across a broad range of drinking levels.
Does Moderate Drinking Have Any Health Benefits?
For years, moderate alcohol consumption has sometimes been promoted as beneficial for cardiovascular health. The new findings cast doubt on that idea when the full range of alcohol-related health effects is considered.
The researchers found no statistically significant protective effect on overall health at any level of alcohol consumption.
They acknowledged that relatively low alcohol intake may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. Ischemic heart disease occurs when reduced blood flow deprives the heart muscle of the oxygen it needs, often because arteries have narrowed or become blocked.
However, any potential cardiovascular benefits must be considered alongside alcohol's association with cancer, liver disease, injuries, and other serious conditions.
When the researchers combined these outcomes, the potential benefits were outweighed by the harmful effects, even among people consuming seven alcoholic drinks per week.
This broader assessment helps explain why a drinking habit that appears beneficial when examining one disease may still increase overall health risks.
Alcohol Risks Vary From Person to Person
Although the findings offer a clearer picture of the long-term dangers of alcohol, the researchers emphasize that the estimates describe risks across populations, not the precise likelihood that any individual will develop a particular disease.
The statistical models relied on "the best possible data," according to the research team. Nevertheless, personal health outcomes can differ considerably depending on genetics, lifestyle, drinking patterns, and other individual factors.
To calculate the overall burden of alcohol consumption, the investigators estimated risks for health conditions already known to have a causal relationship with drinking. They then combined those estimates to assess the total impact.
The researchers also acknowledged that scientific understanding of alcohol's health effects continues to evolve. Emerging evidence suggests that drinking may be associated with additional conditions, including pancreatic cancer, that require further investigation.
"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," said Keyes and Shield.
Despite these uncertainties, the results offer an important reference point: alcohol consumption above one drink per day was associated with increased health risks for both men and women.
The researchers believe that giving people more specific information about these risks can help them make better decisions about how much they drink.
"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking."
Why the Findings Matter for U.S. Alcohol Guidelines
The research also raises questions about how scientific evidence is considered when federal drinking recommendations are developed.
In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former associate administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, discussed the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the federal dietary guidance process.
"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."
Vincent's comments highlight concerns about whether the research received appropriate consideration during the development of national recommendations.
The study's findings reinforce the importance of understanding alcohol's cumulative health effects rather than assuming that moderate consumption is beneficial or risk-free. Although individual risks vary, the overall pattern was clear: greater alcohol consumption was associated with greater harm, and the researchers found no overall health advantage to drinking.
The research was funded by Synergy Enterprises Inc. and the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sinead George, Timothy S. Naimi, Katherine Keyes, Priscilla Martinez-Matyszczyk, Adam J. Milam, Jürgen Rehm, Alvaro Alonso, Steven Bell, Annie Britton, Laura Llamosas-Falcón, Erin Hobin, Suzanne E. Judd, Amy Justice, Christopher Kahler, Suthat Liangpunsakul, Stephanie K. Jones, Gregory Marcus, Katherine McGlynn, Derek Satre, Mingyang Song, Aaron Peter Thrift, Tomoko Udo, Ashley Wettlaufer, Zuo-Feng Zhang, Kevin Shield. Alcohol Intake and Health Study: No Protective Effect at Low Levels, With Mortality Increasing to 1 in 25 at 14 Drinks Per Week. articles.title: Tại sao con người hiện đại ngày càng tin ma quỷ?
articles.text:
Ma quỷ, chưa có một bằng chứng nào về sự tồn tại của chúng nhưng số người tin vào ma quỷ sẽ khiến bạn bất ngờ. Có một câu hỏi được đặt ra: Điều gì khiến chúng ta cả tin vào những chuyện hoàn toàn không có cơ sở như vậy?
Theo kết quả của do công ty nghiên cứu thị trường do YouGov thực hiện và cung cấp với sự tham gia của 2.000 người, theo đơn đặt hàng của Hội nghiên cứu khoa học về hiện tượng dị thường (Assap).
52% số người tham gia cho biết họ tin vào các thế lực siêu nhiên. Đây là một sự gia tăng đáng kể so với hai cuộc nghiên cứu trong năm 2009 và 2005, khi con số này chỉ khoảng 40%.
(Ảnh: threatquality.com)
Một phần nào đó, nhiều người trong chúng ta tin vào ma quỷ chỉ đơn giản là do cách não của chúng ta làm việc, Barry Markovsky - nhà xã hội học tại Đại học South Carolina (Mỹ) cho biết. Tâm trí con người luôn hướng tới một mô hình có ý nghĩa của những thông tin không rõ ràng.
(Ảnh: Businessinsider).
"Ma gần như luôn được 'nhìn thấy' trong những hoàn cảnh không thật sự rõ ràng, chẳng hạn như trong điều kiện ánh sáng kém, hoặc khi chúng ta vừa thức dậy hoặc ngủ thiếp đi, lúc mà các giác quan của chúng ta không phải đang trong trạng thái ổn định nhất", Markovsky nói.
Những người tin vào ma quỷ thường sẵn sàng tâm thế để chuẩn bị cho các tình huống mà họ mong đợi để nhìn thấy ma, giả dụ như trong một ngôi nhà bị "ma ám". Nói cách khác, nếu bạn đang tìm kiếm thứ gì đó, nhiều khả năng bạn sẽ tìm thấy nó.
Một loạt các niềm tin siêu nhiên tồn tại trong những nền văn hóa khác nhau, tuy nhiên 'bóng ma' có lẽ là thứ phổ biến nhất, theo Benjamin Radford, phó tổng biên tập của tạp chí khoa học Skeptical Inquirer và tác giả của cuốn "Scientific Paranormal Investigation: How to Solve Unexplained Mysteries" (tạm dịch: Khám phá sự huyền bí theo khoa học: Làm thế nào để giải quyết các bí ẩn khó hiểu).
(Ảnh: livescience).
Một phần nguyên do dẫn đến sự hình thành niềm tin vào ma quỷ có thể xuất phát từ niềm tin vào thế giới bên kia, một nguyên lý của hầu hết các tôn giáo lớn. Tin vào năng lực siêu nhiên cũng có nguồn gốc từ những ước muốn có quyền kiểm soát thế giới của chúng ta, Radford giải thích. Rốt cuộc, thế giới là nơi mà những điều ngẫu nhiên xảy ra là một cách đáng sợ.
Một cuộc thăm dò của Gallup cho thấy ở khu vực châu Phi cận Sahara, hơn một nửa số người được khảo sát tin vào phép thuật, và những người này thường có xu hướng đánh giá mình kém hạnh phúc hơn so với những người không tin vào điều đó. Ngoài ra, một nghiên cứu năm 2008 cũng phát hiện ra rằng những người cô đơn có nhiều khả năng tin vào năng lực siêu nhiên.
Một cảnh trong phim Paranormal Activity. (Ảnh: Youtube).
Tất nhiên, một lý do khác khiến mọi người tin có ma cũng giống nhau việc lý giải vì sao mọi người thích xem phim kinh dị hay chơi cầu cơ: tìm kiễm nỗi sợ. Về cơ bản, mọi người thực hiện điều này vì họ biết rằng họ đang không ở trong bất kỳ mối nguy hiểm thực sự nào, Radford cho biết. Nhưng có một mâu thuẫn tâm điểm của niềm tin vào ma quỷ. Một mặt, có ý kiến cho rằng bóng ma đáng sợ và muốn làm hại chúng ta, nhưng mặt khác, có những người tìm kiếm những bóng ma.
Nhiều thợ săn ma xem mình là "cảnh sát giao thông cho thế giới bên kia", theo Radford. Thay vì tin rằng ma thường mang đến điều dữ, họ nghĩ về chúng như những linh hồn, mà đơn giản chỉ là đang đi một con đường khác so với con người. Như Radford nói: "Nếu bạn thật sự sợ hãi các bóng ma và nghĩ rằng họ có thể giết bạn, vậy cớ gì bạn lại đi tìm kiếm họ?". Tất nhiên, các bộ phim và chương trình truyền hình về ma hay săn ma thường được trình bày với rất ít sự hoài nghi và không có ích gì. Nếu chỉ mang tính vui vẻ thì nó thật sự tốt, nhưng Radford cũng nhắc nhở: "Đừng tin tất cả những gì bạn nhìn thấy trên truyền hình!"
Một trong những lý do mạnh mẽ nhất khiến con người tin vào ma quỷ chính là yếu tố cảm xúc. Nỗi sợ về cái chết và nỗi đau mất đi người thân là những cảm xúc rất con người và luôn hiện diện. Ý tưởng rằng chúng ta hoặc người thân có thể “tiếp tục tồn tại” dưới một hình thức khác sau khi chết giúp chúng ta vơi đi nỗi sợ và an ủi tâm hồn. Giáo sư danh dự Chris French thuộc Đơn vị Nghiên cứu Dị thường tại Goldsmiths, Đại học London nói rằng dù ông không tin vào các yếu tố siêu nhiên, nhưng ông cũng không ngăn cản người khác duy trì niềm tin của họ nếu nó mang lại sự an tâm và tích cực trong cuộc sống.
Bên cạnh các yếu tố văn hóa và cảm xúc, bộ não con người đôi khi cũng khiến chúng ta hiểu lầm về các hiện tượng tự nhiên. Những tiếng động nhỏ hay những sự việc ngẫu nhiên có thể nhanh chóng được não bộ liên kết với các thế lực huyền bí. Bộ não của chúng ta vốn được “lập trình” để tự lý giải các hiện tượng không quen thuộc và có thể dễ dàng làm cho chúng ta tin rằng chúng ta không hề đơn độc.

articles.title: NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past
articles.text:
NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the solar system’s origins by studying 27 tiny, distant objects beyond Neptune. Scientists discovered that these ancient building blocks of planets have remained remarkably unchanged for billions of years, while their unexpected sizes and numbers challenge existing theories of planet formation.
- Share:
NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the earliest days of our solar system by examining some of the smallest and faintest objects ever observed beyond Neptune. The findings challenge expectations about how planets form and suggest that these distant, icy bodies have preserved evidence of their origins for billions of years.
For the first time, astronomers combined observations from Hubble and Webb to investigate trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), tiny bodies that travel around the Sun far beyond Neptune's orbit. Researchers discovered 27 previously unknown objects, but their findings revealed an unexpected puzzle. There were fewer small objects than some theories predicted, and their colors closely resembled those of much larger objects in the same distant regions.
These frozen remnants offer a rare opportunity to study the materials that eventually became planets. Most are extraordinarily difficult to detect, shining more than 100 million times more faintly than objects visible to the naked eye. Two related studies published in The Astronomical Journal examined the newly identified objects to learn more about their sizes, compositions, and ancient history.
Ancient Building Blocks of the Solar System
Scientists believe planets began forming when tiny particles of dust and pebbles orbiting the young Sun gradually accumulated into larger bodies. Over time, these materials formed objects roughly the size of cities, known as "planetesimals." These early building blocks eventually combined to create the planets we see today.
However, that final stage of growth did not occur for many objects beyond Neptune. Instead of developing into full-sized planets, countless smaller bodies remained, preserving evidence of the solar system's earliest period of formation.
To investigate these distant survivors, research teams led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria in Canada, working under the guidance of the National Research Council of Canada, and Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff conducted the deepest survey of trans-Neptunian objects to date. Both space telescopes observed the same region of sky simultaneously, with Hubble collecting visible light and Webb capturing infrared light.
By combining these observations, astronomers could examine the objects' colors, estimate their sizes, and determine how they orbit the Sun. Their colors are especially valuable because they provide clues about the chemical makeup of their surfaces, much like fingerprints that reveal an object's identity and history.
Two Populations of Distant Icy Worlds
The researchers focused on two distinct populations of trans-Neptunian objects, known as dynamically "cold" and dynamically "hot" TNOs. These descriptions refer to their orbital behavior rather than their temperatures.
Cold objects have largely remained in the regions where they originally formed. They follow relatively circular paths around the Sun and stay close to the plane in which most of the solar system's planets orbit.
Hot objects have experienced a much more turbulent history. They originally formed between the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune but were scattered outward as the giant planets shifted positions early in the solar system's development. Their current orbits are much more elongated, and they travel above and below the solar system's main orbital plane.
Despite these dramatically different histories, the two populations revealed an unexpected similarity. Even the smallest objects appear to have retained surface characteristics resembling those of their larger counterparts.
Tiny Worlds Preserve Their Ancient Origins
Before the observations, scientists suspected that smaller TNOs would show clear evidence of repeated collisions over billions of years. Impacts could have fractured the objects and exposed fresh material, potentially changing their surface compositions and colors.
Instead, the newly discovered objects displayed the same general color relationships seen among larger TNOs. This suggests that collisions may have altered their surfaces much less than expected.
One possibility is that these objects have experienced fewer impacts than astronomers previously assumed. Another is that their surfaces somehow retain their original compositions even after collisions. Researchers have not yet determined which explanation is correct.
"You could imagine a scenario where getting knocked around and fragmented would change the surface composition, and then you would see a different surface color for tiny TNOs compared to their larger siblings. So it's really fascinating to see that the smallest objects are somehow 'remembering' and preserving the history of how they were made," said Northern Arizona University PhD candidate Anastasia Morgan, who led the study of color and composition.
"These dynamically 'hot' TNOs retain a signature of where they were born, even though they've been orbitally scrambled since then," said co-author David Trilling of Northern Arizona University.
The observations indicate that both hot and cold TNOs have maintained color patterns linked to their formation, with surprisingly little apparent change since the solar system's beginnings. These ancient objects may therefore preserve important information about the environments in which they first took shape.
Webb Finds Fewer Tiny Worlds Than Expected
The James Webb Space Telescope also provided another important piece of the puzzle. Its observations allowed scientists to examine how many objects exist at different sizes, revealing an unexpected resemblance between the two populations.
Although hot and cold TNOs formed in different parts of the early solar system, their overall size distributions were remarkably alike. This suggests that the processes responsible for creating planetesimals may have operated in much the same way across different environments.
"It's very interesting that the process of planetesimal formation ends up producing the same distribution of sizes for both cold and hot populations, despite forming in different regions of the early solar system. The process seems to be insensitive to disk conditions, producing similar planetesimal sizes whether the disk is hot or cold, and dense or fluffy," said University of Victoria PhD candidate Marielle Eduardo, who led the study on size distribution.
The researchers also identified a surprising shortage of very small TNOs compared with predictions from some existing planet formation models. Understanding why fewer objects were detected could help scientists refine their explanations of how the solar system's original building blocks developed.
Webb's extraordinary sensitivity made it possible to discover 27 exceptionally faint objects. One was so dim that detecting it would be comparable to standing on Earth and spotting a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon.
The smallest object measured just 3 miles (5 kilometers) across, making it approximately five times smaller than the objects detectable with even the most sensitive telescopes on the ground.
Hubble and Webb Reveal New Clues to Planet Formation
These discoveries depended on the complementary capabilities of NASA's two powerful space observatories. Hubble's ability to detect visible light and Webb's sensitivity to infrared light gave scientists a more complete picture of the distant objects than either telescope could have provided independently.
Together, the telescopes have opened a new window into a largely unexplored population of ancient solar system remnants. Their surprising similarities, preserved surface characteristics, and unexpected numbers offer important clues about the processes that shaped the planets billions of years ago.

articles.title: Lycurgus Cup — a Roman glass goblet made with ancient color-changing nanotechnology
articles.text:
Lycurgus Cup: A Roman glass goblet made with ancient color-changing nanotechnology
This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.
QUICK FACTS
Name: Lycurgus Cup
What it is: A glass drinking cup
Where it is from: The Roman Empire
When it was made: Fourth century A.D.
The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.
In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).
The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.
Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.
Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.
For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.
A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.
But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.
For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives.
Can you put together last week's Astonishing Artifact?
Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Rocket Lab launches Japanese Earth-observing satellite on 99th mission to date (video)
articles.text:
Rocket Lab launches Japanese Earth-observing satellite on 99th mission to date (video)
Rocket Lab launched its 99th mission to date today (Nov. 2), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite toward orbit.
An Electron rocket lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site today at 11:41 a.m. EST (1641 GMT; 5:41 a.m. on Nov. 3 local New Zealand time).
The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Sea God Surveys," is carrying an Earth-observing radar satellite to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Japanese company iQPS. All went according to plan: The spacecraft was deployed at an altitude of 357 miles (575 kilometers), Rocket Lab announced about 56 minutes after launch.
"The Sea God Surveys" was Rocket Lab's 10th launch to date for iQPS, which is assembling a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO.
SAR satellites offer advantages over those that view our planet in optical wavelengths. They can peer through cloud cover, for example, and study our planet at night as well as during the day.
Today's launch was the 99th overall for Rocket Lab and the 90th for the two-stage, 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron, which gives small satellites dedicated rides to space. The workhorse vehicle has now flown 17 times this year.
Rocket Lab's other nine launches to date have been conducted by HASTE, a suborbital version of Electron that allows customers to test their tech in the hypersonic flight environment. HASTE (short for "Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron") debuted in June 2023 and generally flies classified payloads.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:55 a.m. ET on Nov. 2 with news of successful launch, then again at 1 p.m. EST with news of successful satellite deployment.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
articles.text:
Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
A major new review casts doubt on medical cannabis as a sleep aid, finding surprisingly little reliable evidence that it helps people with insomnia.
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- Cochrane
- Summary:
- A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.
- Share:
A major new scientific review is raising questions about whether medical cannabis actually helps people with insomnia. Despite growing interest in cannabis as a sleep treatment, researchers found that the available evidence is too weak to reliably determine whether it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or how well people function during the day.
Insomnia affects millions of people and can make it difficult to fall asleep, remain asleep throughout the night, or wake up feeling rested. Beyond the frustration of sleepless nights, the condition can seriously disrupt daily life and increase the likelihood of developing anxiety or depression.
Treatments for insomnia include cognitive behavioral therapy, which helps people change thoughts and habits that interfere with sleep, as well as medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. However, these approaches do not work equally well for everyone, fueling interest in alternative options.
Medical cannabis has attracted particular attention because of its potential to improve sleep. Unlike recreational cannabis, regulated medical products typically contain carefully measured amounts of THC and CBD, two compounds found in cannabis, and are administered as tablets, sprays, or oils. Despite its growing popularity, scientists have continued to debate whether cannabis offers meaningful benefits for people with insomnia.
Major Review Finds Little Evidence of Sleep Benefits
To investigate, researchers from The Cochrane Associate Centre at the Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and the University of Manitoba examined nine clinical studies involving 537 adults between the ages of 18 and 76 who were receiving treatment for insomnia.
Most of the studies involved people with primary insomnia, meaning their sleep problems were not attributed to another medical condition. Eight trials compared regulated medical cannabis with a placebo, an inactive treatment used to measure whether a therapy produces genuine benefits. The remaining trial compared cannabis with amitriptyline, an antidepressant that is sometimes used to treat sleep problems.
Across the placebo comparisons, medical cannabis produced little or no clinically meaningful improvement in sleep quality, satisfaction with sleep, total hours slept, or daytime functioning.
The researchers also identified potential drawbacks. Participants who received medical cannabis were substantially more likely to experience mild side effects, including dizziness and dry mouth, than those given a placebo. However, this finding came from a relatively small number of studies, limiting confidence in the result.
There was some indication that medical cannabis might improve overall quality of life. Yet the evidence supporting this possibility was highly uncertain. When the findings were combined, the results were consistent with outcomes ranging from a slight decline in quality of life to a substantial improvement.
"The main message is that the research currently available is not sufficient to reliably answer whether medical cannabis helps people with insomnia," says Dr. Lucia Varela, lead author of the study from the University of Manitoba, Canada. "This does not mean that medical cannabis is ineffective. It means that, based on the evidence we have, we cannot draw reliable conclusions about its effectiveness for insomnia in the general population."
Why Scientists Remain Uncertain About Cannabis and Insomnia
One of the biggest problems was the quality of the research itself. The reviewers rated their confidence in the available evidence as low or very low, citing small study populations, conflicting findings, and potential bias in how the trials were conducted.
Another challenge was the lack of consistency between studies. Researchers tested different medical cannabis products, making it difficult to directly compare their results or determine whether particular formulations might work better than others.
The studies were also relatively short. The longest followed participants for just 12 weeks, leaving major unanswered questions about whether medical cannabis could provide lasting sleep benefits or produce additional effects with prolonged use.
More Research Is Needed Before Cannabis Can Be Recommended
The researchers also cautioned that the study participants did not adequately represent the broader population of people living with insomnia.
Women accounted for nearly three-quarters (72.66% of participants), and the research was heavily weighted toward younger adults. As a result, it remains unclear whether the findings would apply equally to men, older individuals, or people whose insomnia occurs alongside other medical conditions.
Taken together, these limitations mean that the existing research cannot establish whether medical cannabis is an effective insomnia treatment. The authors emphasize that larger, more rigorous clinical trials are needed before it can be confidently recommended for improving sleep.
Importantly, the findings do not establish that medical cannabis is ineffective. Instead, they highlight how much remains unknown about a treatment that has gained considerable attention despite limited high-quality evidence.
"The evidence is too weak and uncertain to draw firm conclusions about the use of medical cannabis for insomnia," says Dr. Luis Garegnani, senior author from Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Argentina. "Rather than viewing the findings as either an endorsement or a rejection of medical cannabis, clinicians and patients should recognize the uncertainty and consider individual circumstances while better evidence is generated."
