articles.title: Birdbuddy and Birdfy Want Their Budget Smart Bird Feeders to Be Your First
articles.text:
Hard to believe, but smart bird feeders have been around for six years.
The idea started with Birdbuddy (then styled Bird Buddy), which launched a Kickstarter campaign in November 2020 for the world’s first app-connected, AI-powered smart bird feeder. Birdfy followed in 2021 with its first camera-equipped feeder, and today the two companies remain the most popular brands in the smart bird-feeder space, with a sizable catalog of offerings, including smart bird baths and smart nesting boxes.
Thanks to two new releases from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, you can now get a premium smart bird feeder experience for under $100—something that just a year or two ago would have cost $200 or more.
I tested both Birdfy’s Rookie and Birdbuddy’s Nook in my backyard for four weeks each, noting annoyances, especially helpful features, and which features were available without a subscription.
While both have a significant number of pluses and minuses, Birdbuddy’s Nook, despite costing $20 more and failing to capture every visit, came out just slightly ahead due to its more premium hardware experience.
Birdfy Rookie
Released in October of last year, Birdfy’s Rookie was positioned as a smart feeder for beginners, with USB-C charging only, no solar (though you can buy a more expensive model that has it), and no complicated assembly process. It functions basically as a lightweight gravity pet feeder with a 1.3-liter seed capacity and a camera on the side—just snap the three main pieces together, charge the camera, and you’re good to go. It can only be pole- or wall-mounted, not hung.
While I loved the simplicity of the Rookie and appreciated that it uses the same excellent app as the pricier Birdfy feeders, the 1080p camera’s picture quality was noticeably lower than the Nook’s, and while it did capture every bird that visited, there were also plenty of false-alarm motion detections.
I also found some significant drawbacks to the design over my four-week test. First, though the feeder itself is IP66 rated for water resistance, there’s no overhang on the roof, which means water is going to get into the seed if it rains (as it did off and on throughout my testing period).
Second, the lid just sits loosely on the top, so it kept blowing off whenever there was a big gust of wind. And third, perhaps most frustratingly, because the camera is on the side, it didn’t do the greatest job capturing larger birds, though the camera lens stayed relatively clean, being farther away from the action, and small-bird shots were well framed. Birdfy advertises the battery charge as lasting seven weeks, but my test unit lasted less than two.
One big advantage the Rookie has, however, is its seed capacity. At 1.3 liters, it’s only slightly less voluminous than Birdfy’s popular original feeder, which packs 1.5 liters. (Though note that this still pales in comparison to Birdfy’s Bamboo feeder, a top pick in our guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, which holds 3.5 liters.)
Feeder capacity aside, Birdfy’s app is well designed and simple, and it makes it easy to see which birds visited that day. You can even watch your feeder on TV if you have Roku—the Birdfy app is available on devices running Roku OS 15.1 or higher. Best of all, as of November 1, Birdfy offers unlimited automatic AI-based identification without a subscription, which is a rarity among smart bird feeders. Birdfy’s ID is pretty decent, with nearly no mistakes during my test.
If you want to spring for more storage or longer video recording (free tier is limited to 5 GB and 20 seconds), you can opt for Birdfy Plus for $80/year or Birdfy Pro for $150/year.
Birdbuddy Nook
Birdbuddy’s Nook launched in late October this year and is also aimed at beginners and budget-conscious shoppers. It looks a lot like Birdbuddy’s flagship Home (previously the 2 Pro), just smaller and squatter. It has the same thick plastic construction with a roof to keep out rain, but the Nook’s hinged lid makes filling a breeze. (Note that the $99 version does not come with the extended perch or solar roof, as pictured.)
Like the Home, the camera is a half-sphere about the size of a ping-pong ball that pops in and out with a magnet; you can position it vertically or horizontally depending on which style of photos you prefer. My test unit came with the solar panel, so I was not able to test the battery life of the camera, but know that the Nook’s battery only delivers 3,900 mAh compared to the Rookie’s 5,200 mAh.
The Nook shoots in 2K HDR, resulting in noticeably crisper imagery and sound. Unlike the Rookie’s side camera, the Nook’s is centered on the feeder—which makes for better full-bird shots, but its close proximity means it tends to get dirtier and smudged more easily than the Rookie’s side camera. I was also surprised by how fast the seed disappeared—within a day in some cases. Birdbuddy states that its seed hopper holds 0.9 liters, or 3.8 cups, which is only slightly less than the Rookie, but the difference in empty rates was noticeable.
My test unit also came with the optional Extended Perch for bigger birds like Steller’s jays and crows, though the big birds in my yard have always managed to find a way to visit the Birdbuddy Home, which has Birdbuddy’s usual tiny perch, so I’m not entirely convinced this is worth the extra $40. However, I do like that I can hang the IP67-rated Nook, especially since its pole-mount option doesn’t have a fastener. This means it tends to swing around when it’s mounted on a 1-inch-diameter pole, especially when larger birds land and take off.
Birdbuddy’s strength has always been its app, which remains easy to use and presents a library of shareable photos from each bird visit, though its interface is quickly being bested by newer brands like Kiwibit and even Birdfy, which just began offering AI ID for free with all its feeders. (Birdbuddy’s app also offers free AI ID, which is excellent, but you have to manually engage it for each photo, making it harder to see at a glance which species visited that day.)
Birdbuddy cameras have also historically struggled to capture all bird visits, and while the Nook was advertised to have a faster wake time, it still missed many bird visits I saw, though I did notice more captures than previous models, with no false alarms.
One new feature of the Birdbuddy app—and one I have not seen before—is the ability to ID other birds from sounds in the background, à la Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s Merlin ID app. It currently states it’s a “free preview,” though, so I suspect it will ultimately be locked behind a subscription tier. Still, I found it to be a neat complement to the Nook’s superior onboard microphone. Other features requiring a subscription (Birdbuddy Premium for $70/year or Birdbuddy Family for $99/year) include Ultra resolution, guest access to the livestream, and the ability to name individual birds.
Rookie vs. Nook
| Specs | Birdbuddy Nook | Birdfy Rookie | 
|---|---|---|
| Base-model price | $99 | $80 | 
| Camera | 2K HDR | 1080p | 
| Orientation | Horizontal or vertical | Vertical | 
| Battery | 3,900 mAh rechargeable | 5,200 mAh rechargeable | 
| Camera location | Front | Side | 
| Standard solar charging? | No (available for extra) | No (available for extra) | 
| Seed capacity | 0.9 liters | 1.3 liters | 
| Subscription cost | $70–$99/year | $80–$150/year | 
| AI ID without subscription? | Yes, manual | Yes | 
| Mounting options | Hang, wall, pole | Wall, pole | 
| Supported Wi-Fi networks | 2.4 GHz | 2.4 GHz | 
| Color options | Blue | Tan, blue | 
The Winner: Birdbuddy Nook
If you’re looking to spend under $100, the Rookie is a perfectly respectable smart bird feeder, with excellent free AI ID. However, if you want the whole package, I have to give the edge to the Nook. It won’t show you every bird that visits, which is disappointing, but you’ll get great shots of the ones that do, and its sturdy housing and versatile camera make it a great value that will hold up well in inclement weather.

articles.title: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon | TechCrunch
articles.text:
SpaceX is looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar, according to a report from The Washington Post. If the deal goes through, it would help the Elon Musk-owned company build a hybrid cellular-satellite network that could help catapult it into fourth place among the top U.S. wireless providers.
The space-launch company has been dabbling in cellular connectivity, rolling out satellite access to T-Mobile’s subscribers in 2024. Last year, SpaceX bought $17 billion worth of wireless spectrum from EchoStar for cellular services, which could help the company’s Starlink service reach inside buildings, for example, something it currently struggles with.
“This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk said on X at the time of the spectrum acquisition. Yet, if Musk is still looking to buy access to terrestrial networks, it apparently wasn’t the last piece.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO, reportedly spoke directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen in October about acquiring Boost Mobile, the mobile virtual network operator. EchoStar has about 7.5 million customers between Boost Mobile and Gen Mobile, its other mobile service offering.
Musk has also approached AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon about buying capacity on their networks. All three rejected Musk, and they may still have a say in a SpaceX acquisition of Boost Mobile. Boost doesn’t operate its own towers, instead leasing capacity from AT&T and T-Mobile, which might need to approve such a deal. Sources speaking to The Post said that network leases are usually nontransferable.
The big three providers each have over 100 million subscribers, dwarfing Boost Mobile. But while the acquisition would give SpaceX an immediate bump in subscribers, the true value of the deal would be giving the company access to terrestrial cellular networks.
Gaining access to towers leased to Boost Mobile would expand coverage significantly — Boost currently covers most of the 48 contiguous states in the U.S. — allowing Starlink to cover devices when they’re outdoors and relying on cell towers to handle devices when Starlink signals can’t reach them.

articles.title: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
articles.text:
BMW says that it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow.
BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
BMW will bring navigation-guided city driving to select models via software updates in 2027, taking on Tesla’s FSD while facing growing scrutiny over Level 2 driver safety.
The new system can help steer, speed up, and slow down the vehicle on both highways and city streets using its built-in GPS navigation. While driving in town, it can assist with changing lanes, making turns, yielding to other cars, and driving through roundabouts. But as a Level 2 driver assist system, it still requires drivers to keep their eyes on the road and stay ready to take over at any moment. On the highway, BMW will allow drivers to remove their hands from the steering wheel — but on local roads, they’ll need to keep their hands on the wheel.
BMW is the latest automaker to commit to releasing a partially autonomous city driving feature to its customers, as the industry races to keep up with Tesla and its Full Self-Driving (FSD) system. BMW, in particular, recently introduced its next-generation Neue Klasse platform, which includes a driver assist system partly powered by Qualcomm’s technology. And with hands-free highway driving now widely available in many mass-market vehicles, the next frontier is a safe and capable city driving feature that rivals FSD.
BMW says its system works cooperatively with drivers rather than fighting their control, which means they can steer, brake, or speed up at any point to adjust their driving without shutting the system off. At the same time, the car shows what it sees and what the assistance system is doing right in your line of sight through the heads-up display and in a clear 3D map on the main dashboard screen.
The necessary cameras and sensors already come built into models like BMW’s 3 Series, 7 Series, X5, iX3, and iX4. BMW can activate the feature through an over-the-air software update. The system follows new European safety rules that let cars suggest and make automated driving moves on city streets for the first time. BMW says that outside experts have already road-tested the setup and confirmed it meets the technical standards, with final official government approval expected in early 2027.
With more cars equipped with partial automation hitting the road, safety researchers are growing increasingly worried about driver attention and the potential for these systems to cause crashes. There is compelling evidence that, regardless of the company, most driver-assist systems are less safe than normal human driving. Drivers tend to develop an overreliance on these systems to drive the car for them — even after a short period of use. And when it’s time to take back control of the vehicle, their reaction times are slower than what’s considered safe.
BMW is entering risky territory with the adoption of a Level 2 driving feature. Much like Tesla, the company is emphasizing that drivers remain responsible for the vehicle even while using the partially autonomous system in urban environments. Tesla does the same for its FSD feature, but some customers have successfully argued in court that the company bears some responsibility for crashes when they occur.

articles.title: New Zealand’s central bank registers Revolut as the country’s 27th bank
articles.text:
Revolut has been registered as a bank in New Zealand, clearing the way for the fintech to expand its financial services in the country.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand announced the approval on Tuesday, local time, making Revolut Bank New Zealand the country’s 27th registered bank.
The London-based company has operated in New Zealand since July 2023. When it applied for registration in late 2024, it said approval would make it the first global digital bank in the country. It plans to introduce interest-paying savings accounts and a broader range of credit products.
“The Reserve Bank recognises the value that credible new entrants can bring,” said Scott McKinnon, the central bank’s director of specialist supervision.
He added that new banks can make the financial system more competitive, resilient and inclusive. However, the registration process remains rigorous, with every applicant assessed against the same banking requirements.
Revolut NZ has been registered under New Zealand’s current banking legislation. The framework will be replaced by the Deposit Takers Act, which is due to come into force on 1 December 2028, the central bank said.
“Launching our New Zealand bank marks another significant step in our mission to build the world’s first truly global bank. Securing our seventh bank licence and our fifth this year alone is a testament to our business model and our team. We are confident our offering will bring true competition to the New Zealand banking sector,” said Nik Storonsky, Founder and CEO of Revolut
The approval adds to a series of banking licence wins for Revolut over the past year. In March, the company secured its full UK banking licence after a multi-year wait.
In July, Australia’s regulator granted it an unrestricted banking licence, its first in the Asia-Pacific region. Revolut said it planned to invest A$400m to challenge Australia’s Big Four banks.
New Zealand’s banking market is dominated by the same four Australian banking groups, giving Revolut another opportunity to compete with established lenders. Matt Baxby, the company’s chief executive for Australia and New Zealand, has described the country as prime ground for expansion.
When Revolut applied for registration, it said it had more than 50 million customers worldwide. Its New Zealand business had already processed over NZ$350m in transactions by late 2024.
The expansion comes as Revolut continues to build its international presence ahead of a possible public listing. The company was valued at $75bn in a share sale last year, making it Europe’s most valuable private tech company.

articles.title: Microsoft and Lumen will jointly sell networks built for AI on Azure
articles.text:
Microsoft and Lumen Technologies are expanding their partnership to jointly sell networking to companies running AI on Azure. Lumen plans to bring its full cloud networking range to Azure. No figures or dates were given.
Microsoft and Lumen Technologies will jointly sell networking to large companies moving their AI work onto Azure, the two firms said on Monday.
Their pitch is that AI needs data from many places, such as public clouds, private data centres and offices. The networks linking them are often patchy, so the firms want customers to plan the network and the move to Azure at the same time.
Lumen, a US fibre network operator, plans to bring its full range of cloud networking tools to Azure. Its sales teams will work with Microsoft’s on deals where networking, cloud moves and AI overlap. AI has also lifted demand for fibre networks, which network-equipment maker Ciena says it can barely meet.
“AI is reshaping where applications run and how organizations use and move data,” said Katy Brown, a corporate vice president at Microsoft.
For now, customers can already buy one Lumen product, Alkira, through Microsoft’s online store for business software. Lumen bought Alkira, which lets firms manage links between clouds and offices from one place, for $475M earlier this year.
The firms also plan to explore how their networks could work with Microsoft’s tools for controlling AI agents. They gave no figures or timeline.
The deal builds on a 2024 tie-up in which Lumen supplies fibre links between Microsoft’s data centres. Azure passed $100B in yearly sales in July.

articles.title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can 'predict human behavior' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?
Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.
“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.
“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.
42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.
“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”
“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.
The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.)
Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured.
42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said.
In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity.
In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.
He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.)
And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.
Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.
Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.
The $62.5 million seed funding came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years, and wasn’t entirely raised from external investors, Gal-Or said. Infinity was founded by his father, Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI’s chairman and a co-founder. 42AI now plans to raise more money.
Beyond finance, 42AI is now exploring applications for its model in gaming, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity, and one day wants to use it to help robots and AI agents understand people. But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.
And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: If a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring, and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.
Amit Gal-Or, however, was confident that the technology could help address such risks. “We are very proud that actually we are part of the solution; we are the solution to this problem,” he said.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 2/11: Thế giới giảm, trong nước chờ tuần mới
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Mở cửa phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (2/11), giá dầu thế giới có xu hướng đi xuống.
Dữ liệu từ Oilprice cho hay, vào lúc 6h53' ngày 2/11 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent được niêm yết ở mức 111,6 USD/thùng, giảm 1,62% so với phiên liền trước. Còn giá dầu WTI được giao dịch ở mức 102,3 USD/thùng, hạ 1,76% so với phiên liền trước.
Trong tuần trước, giá dầu thế giới ghi nhận tuần biến động trái chiều khi giá dầu Brent hạ còn dầu WTI tăng.
Tính chung trong cả tuần qua, giá dầu Brent hạ 3,3 USD/thùng, trong khi giá dầu WTI tăng 0,8 USD/thùng.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần qua ở mức 113,4 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần trước ở mức 104,1 USD/thùng.
Trong tuần này, dù có xu hướng suy yếu khi mở cửa phiên giao dịch đầu tuần nhưng giá dầu thế giới vẫn duy trì ở mức cao trên 100 USD/thùng trong bối cảnh thị trường tiếp tục chịu tác động từ những lo ngại về căng thẳng địa chính trị tại Trung Đông, đặc biệt là nguy cơ xung đột giữa Mỹ và Iran leo thang sau cuộc bầu cử giữa nhiệm kỳ tại Mỹ.
Những diễn biến an ninh tại Trung Đông tiếp tục làm dấy lên lo ngại về việc các cơ sở năng lượng trong khu vực có thể trở thành mục tiêu tấn công, đe dọa hoạt động khai thác, vận chuyển và xuất khẩu dầu thô.
Theo báo cáo công bố vào ngày 29/10 của ngân hàng Saxo Bank (Đan Mạch), giá dầu có thể biến động mạnh hơn trong vài tuần tới do tác động từ cuộc bầu cử gần đây tại Israel và cuộc bầu cử giữa nhiệm kỳ của Mỹ vào ngày 3/11.
Ngân hàng này dự báo, ngay cả khi xung đột kết thúc, giá dầu thô vẫn có thể giao dịch trong vùng giá cao hơn, khoảng 70-90 USD/thùng, so với mức 60-70 USD/thùng trước xung đột.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date

articles.title: When You Should—and Shouldn’t—Use AI to Search the Web
articles.text:
If you've interacted with the likes of Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, you've noticed that in addition to everything else they do, these AI chatbots can search the web for you. Depending on what you’re looking for, it can be easier to find more relevant results through a chatbot, which may explain why Google is so keen to push AI Mode for its own search engine.
When asked to search the web, the latest versions of these bots are combining elements of traditional web search (they're essentially just googling on your behalf) with knowledge they are able to pull out of their training data. Everything is then packaged and formatted in the now-familiar, polished generative AI style.
It's the added AI elements on top of the traditional googling where the differences come in, and that means AI-powered search may not always be the best option.
When to Use AI for Web Search
If you're looking up something simple and widely known—like the height of the Empire State Building—then AI search is a pretty safe bet. Not only is information like this easy to access online, the “autocorrect” probability patterns favored by large language models mean there's a near-certain chance that the results you see will include the right information.
If you just need a quick look-up, AI is OK. The more obscure the question, though, the closer you need to look at the answer. If you've asked something less well known, like the fifth-billed actor in an obscure television show, there might only be one or two references to it on the web, and an AI might choose the wrong one.
One of the takeaways from recent Stanford University research is that when AI finds an accurate source, it's very good at pulling the right information out of it. Where it tends to fall down is in not finding accurate sources (either because there aren't any or because the query has been misinterpreted) and presenting a confident answer anyway.
AI search is also helpful when you have a complex query that a standard Google search wouldn't be able to parse: "I need to know the best restaurants in San Francisco for a family of five who want to spend no more than $200." AI is able to query and collate multiple sources in response to a search like this, and then present a well-synthesized answer. A traditional web search would give you a list of blue links that most probably just rank San Francisco restaurants by more basic criteria.
Again though, sources are crucial. AI bots have never been to San Francisco or eaten there. They are relying on public accounts on the web, written by people who have. Where there are no exact page matches, they'll look for related words (like "affordable" or "family") and generate an answer.
For queries where there's lots of information online, like San Francisco restaurants, AI web search can feel incredibly useful. For less popular destinations and more specific requests ("dining tables shaped like stars"), you need to be more careful with the results, as the way that AI joins the dots then becomes less reliable.
So, with the caveat that you should always do some kind of double-check, AI web search works best for common queries that are likely to lead to a lot of accurate, up-to-date information online. In both the way they process search queries, and package together and synthesize answers, AI chatbots are a significant upgrade on googling.
When Not to Use AI for Web Search
The way generative AI bots and LLMs are put together means they work best when paraphrasing, synthesizing, and summarizing. But these processes can also introduce mistakes. If your search needs precise details (like a celebrity quotation, a report stat, or a device specification), a traditional Google search may work best.
Heading to Google and searching the old way is also likely to be better if you want full control over the sources used. Offloading web searches to AI is convenient, but you're relying on them to interpret your search correctly, find the right sources, and then extract accurate information from those sources. It saves time, but it's more opaque.
If you know the websites you trust most for technology news, for example, you can prioritize them in a traditional web search in a way that AI might not be able to. Researchers from UC San Diego have found that AI web searches will sometimes pick sources because they're more relevant to the query, rather than because they're ranked as more authoritative.
That means a personal blog might get chosen above a professional health care site if the AI deems it to be a closer match to what the user is actually searching for. This is a choice that you would be much less likely to make when scanning a traditional list of results, as you'd typically pick the one you trusted the most.
Other areas where traditional searching still wins out are for breaking news (there can sometimes be a lag in the timeliness of the data AI pulls up) and for high-stakes searches where you absolutely cannot make a mistake—searches related to health, the law, or your finances, for instance.
If you do feel like an AI approach is needed, be sure to double- and triple-check the sources the chatbot has used, which should be linked inside the answer. If you're in any doubt, you can ask the AI for clarification on where something was sourced from, to make sure it isn't an LLM invention.
Classic Google searches can still turn up false information on the web, of course, but you're in a much better position to discern what's true and accurate and what isn't without a chatbot in the middle. For queries where that's more important than convenience and speed, there's still a place for the old way of searching the web.

articles.title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to 'unsustainably high' costs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: Their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight. Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100%.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.
“The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply to a question from a user. He has not addressed the issue on his main feed but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.
Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income. Its renamed “Super Intelligence” division actually turned a profit of $431 million, which is a rarity in the AI industry. Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor. Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”
Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.

articles.title: Anthropic's message threads let Claude agents skip resending chats
articles.text:
Anthropic launched message threads in public beta for its API. Agents send the full conversation once, then only new messages, which Anthropic says cuts the wait before Claude replies by about 35% on very long sessions. Prices and rate limits stay the same.
Anthropic has launched message threads, a beta feature for developers building AI agents on Claude, the company said on Monday. Agents no longer have to resend the whole conversation every time they make a request.
A coding agent can make hundreds of requests in one session, and each one normally carries every earlier message and tool result. Once that history runs to hundreds of thousands of tokens, sending it all again adds a delay before Claude starts to reply.
With threads, an agent sends the full conversation once. After that, it sends only what is new, plus the ID of Claude’s last reply.
Anthropic has already switched threads on for most users of Claude Code, its coding agent. On requests of 500,000 to 1M tokens, it says the typical wait before Claude starts answering fell by about 35%.
The feature saves time, not money. Claude still reads the whole conversation on every turn, and Anthropic says prices and rate limits are unchanged. On cost, Anthropic instead cut cache prices by 75% in September, as long agent sessions push up AI bills.
Threads are held in memory, encrypted and never written to disk. They expire five minutes after the last request, so developers must keep their own copy of each conversation. Anthropic says threads are not eligible for its zero data retention or HIPAA health-data setups.
The beta works on all Claude models, on Anthropic’s own platform as well as through AWS, Microsoft Foundry and Google Cloud. It follows Anthropic’s cheaper Opus 5.5 model, released in September.

articles.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
articles.text:
Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.
Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
Following GM’s $220 million settlement, Ford promises to never sell customer driving data to data brokers, attempting to set itself apart in an industry rife with tracking.
As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.
In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”
“We know that trust is earned.”
— Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer
The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.
Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.
In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.
Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.
To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

articles.title: Want to Sign With a Hollywood Agent? Start Making Fun of AI
articles.text:
“Hi there!” says an AI avatar of a clean-cut man dressed casually in a denim shirt, with a mostly empty bookcase in the background. “I’m Clark from Marlow & Finch. To get us started, why don’t you tell me a bit about yourself?”
The real human on the other end of the call—Graham Raabe, in glasses and ball cap—is more than ready to dive in. “Happy to, and happy to be here,” he tells his AI job interviewer. “I’m Chick Bongo. I’ve spent about 10 years in sales. Really good at managing badger margin, spent quite a bit of time with sprocket moss, particularly proud of my goosebuckle.”
“Managing badger margin sounds like a serious skill,” the unfazed bot replies. “And that goosebuckle experience is impressive.” Raabe continues to answer Clark’s boilerplate questions with complete nonsense, the fake interviewer echoing most of it in mechanical tones of approval and amazement. When the interviewer inquires what kind of salary range “Chick Bongo” has in mind, Raabe replies, “Six hundred.” Clark interprets this to mean $600,000, calling it a “bold number,” but adds that he admires the “confidence” in the ask.
Raabe isn’t really after a new gig. Actually, in addition to his job as manager of a sales team in the fintech space, he is among a crop of comedians who have recently blown up online—and secured talent representation—by figuring out inventive ways to troll and satirize AI. Absurd, rapid-fire exchanges with agents like Clark have become Raabe’s signature comic routine, one that has doubled his Instagram audience from around 50,000 to more than 100,000 followers over the past two months.
Raabe tells WIRED that he’s been pursuing stand-up comedy and screenwriting as hobbies for the better part of a decade, and trained in improv and sketch at the renowned Upright Citizens Brigade theater. It wasn’t until May of this year, he says, that he started experimenting with office humor videos on Instagram and TikTok.
“I actually didn't start with any AI-adjacent content,” Raabe says. “It was primarily more of a down-the-middle, workplace comedy play, and I was just encouraged by the results and the feedback that I got.”
Raabe has a knack for clever linguistic play, and one of his earlier bits involved substitutions for stock or cliché phrases you might hear in a meeting: instead of “the ball is in your court,” he suggests in one clip, try “the hawk is on your glove” or “that’s your microwave beeping” or “the decision goblin lives at your address.”
Then Raabe started using AI bots to “quiz” him on this type of corporate jargon—his chatbot challenged him, for example, to come up with a euphemism for explaining that his team walked into a meeting unprepared. (“We brought forks to a soup party” was his twist on the phrase.)
Finally, Raabe hit upon the bizarro AI interviewer format. Though he’s never personally endured a bot screening for employment, he was aware of the trend and saw potential in the interview agents from the AI research lab Tavus. (“Screen thousands,” the tool’s marketing copy reads. ”Miss nothing.”) The Tavus bots, Raabe found, could be customized to deliver the conversational rhythms and escalation he needed for a video sketch, and he launched a popular series called “How to Fail Your AI Interview,” in which he derails calls with the avatars with digressive tactics—claiming to have known the bot in college, for example, or insisting on “icebreakers” before the interview begins.
“Most of my comedy is to play off straight men, and AI is the ultimate straight man to improv against,” Raabe explains.
The concept quickly took off, with commenters sharing their own frustrating experiences in real AI interview scenarios. It was around when he began this transition into AI comedy that he gained representation at Dulcedo Management, a talent agency with clients throughout North America, including influencers, models, athletes, and creators. That placed him in a comedy cohort with creators Matt Husk (@husk.irl) and Sam Wassef (@ahh.gpt), two other content creators whose viral AI trolling led to agent deals despite—or perhaps in some way because of—entertainment studios rapidly integrating the tech into production workflows.
Alex Melendez, associate director of gaming and entertainment at Dulcedo, tells WIRED that the company came across Raabe when he had fewer than 10,000 followers and were instantly taken with his sharp timing and original, well-executed premises. As for the AI interview videos, he says that Raabe is mining rich territory.
“There's something inherently funny about the contradiction surrounding AI right now,” Melendez explains. “We're constantly hearing about how it's going to transform industries and replace jobs, and then you see it struggle with something incredibly basic. That disconnect creates a lot of comedic opportunity.” He feels that Raabe and others “are giving audiences a way to laugh at something that can otherwise feel intimidating or overwhelming,” and that the rapid evolution of AI means a steady flow of new material.
“Every development brings another moment that makes people stop and think, ‘What is actually happening?’” Melendez says. “Comedy has always been a way to make sense of cultural shifts, and AI is no exception.”
And though AI may be the butt of these jokes, many tech developers and companies seem to be all for it. “I've gotten multiple DMs from people who are product managers at companies that build AI video avatars like this,” Raabe says. “They've told me that they love to see people having fun with the tools, and occasionally I've gotten messages from product managers who are like, ‘Thanks for pointing out that particular skill gap because now we know how to fix it.’”
Likewise, the surreal and wildly viral dialogues between Matt Husk and OpenAI’s ChatGPT have exposed the weaknesses of the LLM, forcing the company to acknowledge these shortcomings. In his videos, Husk (as he is known across his social media accounts) typically asks the chatbot for some kind of help, with his theoretical problems ranging from drowning in quicksand to simple challenges like counting to a hundred. Without fail, the chatbot cheerfully botches the job, and it tends to gaslight Husk about getting the answer wrong if he presses it to admit fault.
Husk’s content has earned him some 2 million followers combined across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, as well as a deal with the talent agency Unicorn, where he’s represented by Ali Fischbein, founder of the production company Lil Fish Comedy. (Fischbein declined to comment for this article.) And as with Raabe, Husk’s rise as a social media star has coincided with a role as pressure-tester for his favored product.
In April, on the tech podcast Mostly Human, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was prompted to react to a Husk video in which he used ChatGPT as a stopwatch and found that it measured a span of a few seconds as lasting “around 10 minutes.” Altman laughed at the glitch, claiming that it was a “known issue,” and predicted that it would be another year before the voice model could set an accurate timer.
Not everyone in this scene is examining areas where AI might be improved, however. Sam Wassef, who has more than 860,000 followers as @ahh.gpt on Instagram, instead embodies a humanoid parody of a chatbot, delivering a pitch-perfect impression of the inanities and non sequiturs you’ve come to expect from these pioneering models, often while guzzling water by the gallon. Wassef’s shorts featuring this blathering character make up a mysterious countdown—he is a third of the way through a planned run of a hundred posts—and have expanded to cinematic scope. One of the latest videos sees him prattle on about the bright future of AI as the camera gradually reveals that he is standing alone in the center of a barren mall among dark, empty storefronts.
Wassef is signed with talent managers Mikayla Haycock and Adam Loria at Night Media, who declined to comment for this article. Their involvement is more evidence that the entertainment world is looking for people with inventive angles on the AI zeitgeist, which, as Melendez says, is an indicator that they can apply the same comedic skill set to other topics and platforms. The ultimate goal for a client like Raabe, Husk, or Wassef, he explains, “is for audiences to become invested” in them as a performer, not just “the format or trend” that gave them their start. The name of the game is growth and longevity regardless of where public discourse may go next.
“Virality can open the door,” he says, “but it's the talent behind it that builds a lasting career.”

articles.title: Du khách Việt gặp sự cố ở Nhật Bản, Bảo hiểm AAA chi trả gần 480 triệu đồng
articles.text:
Chi trả quyền lợi qua các trường hợp thực tế
Tháng 5/2026, bà Nông Thị V. (sinh năm 1965) đi du lịch tại Thành phố Osaka phải cấp cứu vì viêm thanh quản phù nề cấp, thực hiện thủ thuật mở khí quản và điều trị nội trú gần 10 ngày. Trước chuyến đi, bà tham gia bảo hiểm du lịch toàn cầu của Bảo hiểm AAA với mức phí 905.000 đồng. Sau khi về nước bà đã được chi trả khoảng 479,6 triệu đồng cho chi phí y tế và trợ cấp nằm viện tại Nhật Bản sau 6 ngày hoàn tất hồ sơ theo yêu cầu.
Không chỉ các chuyến đi xa, những sự cố trong hoạt động thường ngày cũng có thể phát sinh những chi phí lớn. Tháng 4/2026, anh Nguyễn Đức H. (sinh năm 1978) bị ngã khi chơi pickleball. Sau 3 ngày, cơn đau và sưng gối không thuyên giảm, anh đi khám và được chẩn đoán đứt dây chằng chéo trước, rách sụn chêm gối trái, phải phẫu thuật. Với mức phí tham gia bảo hiểm sức khỏe Bảo hiểm AAA khoảng 9,88 triệu đồng, anh đã được chi trả 66,2 triệu đồng cho chi phí y tế và khoản trợ cấp cho thời gian nghỉ điều trị.
Hai trường hợp khác là chị Nguyễn N.T. (sinh năm 1999) điều trị u nang buồng trứng và chị Nguyễn T.T. (sinh năm 1992) điều trị bệnh tuyến giáp. Cùng tham gia bảo hiểm sức khỏe với mức phí khoảng 4,19 triệu đồng, hai khách hàng đã lần lượt nhận quyền lợi khoảng 50,5 triệu đồng và 55,2 triệu đồng.
Các trường hợp trên cho thấy bảo hiểm không chỉ giúp chia sẻ chi phí điều trị mà còn tạo thêm nguồn lực tài chính cho khách hàng khi sức khỏe gặp vấn đề.
Đồng hành cùng khách hàng trong quá trình xử lý tổn thất
Bên cạnh quyền lợi chi trả, quy trình tiếp nhận và xử lý sự cố cũng là một khía cạnh thể hiện giá trị của bảo hiểm. Với Bảo hiểm AAA, sự hỗ trợ được triển khai từ khâu ghi nhận thông tin, giám định thiệt hại đến phối hợp sửa chữa và giải quyết bồi thường.
Chị Nguyễn Thị M.N. gặp sự cố khi chiếc ô tô mới mua được 5 ngày va vào cột sắt mái che lúc ra khỏi cổng, khiến phần đầu xe bị hư hỏng. Sau khi nhận tin báo, giám định viên Bảo hiểm AAA nhanh chóng liên hệ hướng dẫn, đến hiện trường ghi nhận thiệt hại và phối hợp đưa xe đến gara sửa chữa. Sau khi hoàn tất sửa chữa, Bảo hiểm AAA bảo lãnh thanh toán khoảng 59,9 triệu đồng.
Trong một trường hợp khác, chiếc Mercedes của chị Lê Thị T.M. (Nha Trang) bị ngập nước thời gian dài khiến xe hư hỏng nặng trong đợt lũ tháng 11/2025. Thời điểm đó các gara đều quá tải, nhiều phụ tùng khan hiếm và phải đặt từ nước ngoài, khiến thời gian sửa chữa kéo dài. Trung tâm Giám định Bồi thường (TTGĐBT) đã cử nhân sự đến Nha Trang gặp trực tiếp khách hàng. Sau khi trao đổi đã đưa ra phương án bồi thường bằng tiền để khách hàng chủ động khắc phục với chi phí quyền lợi 700 triệu đồng.
Đằng sau những kết quả trên, quy trình hỗ trợ 24/7 của Bảo hiểm AAA, từ tiếp nhận thông tin, hướng dẫn khách hàng đến điều phối giám định và theo dõi hồ sơ cũng được khách hàng đặc biệt quan tâm.
Theo ông Phạm Việt Phương, Giám đốc Ban Bảo hiểm Xe cơ giới kiêm phụ trách TTGĐBT, với các sự cố ở khu vực xa hoặc xe không thể di chuyển, Bảo hiểm AAA phối hợp giữa giám định viên các chi nhánh và chuyên quản giám định tại TTGĐBT để hỗ trợ khách hàng.
Tháng 7/2026, Claim247 và AAA247 - hai ứng dụng sử dụng công nghệ AI để hỗ trợ công tác giám định từ xa - đã được triển khai trên toàn hệ thống, số hóa quy trình từ tiếp nhận tổn thất đến đề nghị bồi thường. Trước đó, tháng 12/2025, Bảo hiểm AAA đã ký hợp tác toàn diện với Công ty VETC - đơn vị triển khai và vận hành hệ thống thu phí tự động ETC (Electronic Toll Collection) tại Việt Nam - về cứu hộ; đồng thời Bảo hiểm AAA cũng hoàn thiện chức năng cứu hộ tự động trên AAA247, hướng tới việc rút ngắn thời gian tiếp cận hiện trường, chỉ trong khoảng 30 phút.
Từ một ca cấp cứu nơi đất khách, chấn thương khi chơi thể thao đến ô tô gặp tai nạn, ngập lũ… đều là những rủi ro bất ngờ có thể kéo theo gánh nặng tài chính lớn. Qua các trường hợp thực tế được Bảo hiểm AAA chi trả, giá trị của bảo hiểm không chỉ nằm ở khoản bồi thường, mà còn ở cách doanh nghiệp hỗ trợ khách hàng từ lúc phát sinh sự cố đến khi hoàn tất quyền lợi.

articles.title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition | TechCrunch
articles.text:
U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year — and that number is expected to triple in the next five years, according to The Water Foundation.
That’s an expensive and politically tricky proposition for investors throwing billions of dollars at the challenge of scaling up AI. One way to use less water is to do a better job monitoring the cooling fluids, a task that currently involves sending samples away to a laboratory for tests in a multi-day process.
Omen AI was founded in 2024 to solve that problem. The company is building a real-time sensor to determine whether valves were failing, or if bacteria growth in the system threatened to choke off water flow. After raising a $31 million Series A in June, Omen is now acquiring competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal.
The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs’ CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology: Omen’s sensors looked for elements in the water, while the Aquatic Labs sensor tests its alkalinity.
Putting those two technologies in the same sensor creates a “much richer picture of the water and the fluid,” Adams told TechCrunch, while uniting their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process.
The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company.
Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027.
The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up.
Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.”
AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout, sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built.
“We’re working customers on stuff they’re building today or have already built, and so it doesn’t really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago,” Laberge said. “Our view is, if there’s tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.”

articles.title: My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell
articles.text:
My Journey to the Center of America's Political Spam Text Hell
I've gotten nearly 2,000 campaign fundraising texts that were meant for someone else. I tried to find out why—and uncovered a labyrinth of politicians, data brokers, and shady tactics.
Just as my kid is nodding off for the night, it arrives: a ding. It’s Nancy Pelosi, texting to tell me that if I don’t donate $5 immediately, American democracy will basically collapse. A few minutes later, it’s Cory Booker, with an urgent request. Don’t even get me started on James Talarico.
Sometimes I’m driving, or making dinner, or trying to focus on my work, and another three messages arrive. Barack Obama NEEDS me. There’s a critical deadline approaching. A generous donor has offered an 800 percent match. Everything is at stake.
As I was writing that last paragraph, I got a message from Angus, a cat belonging to Sam Forstag, a Democratic congressional candidate in Montana. Angus needed me to know that Sam was out there working to flip Montana’s First Congressional District, taking on his Republican opponent and the wealthy special interests backing him.
I’m not sure what Angus expected me to do about it.
Political fundraising texts are a fact of American life. They’re intrusive, melodramatic, and relentless.
This year alone, I’ve received 725.
In the first 20 days of October, more than 190 arrived—nearly 10 a day.
On October 14, I got 21.
The strangest part is that most of these messages aren’t meant for me.
They’re meant for a family member who I’ll call John, for privacy reasons. John lives in California and has made small donations to Democrats. I live in New York and have made no political donations at all. We have different names, phone numbers, and bank accounts—a distinction that has apparently proven difficult for a substantial portion of the American political fundraising industry.
For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.
When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.
Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?
For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.
James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.
The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.
In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.
I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.
Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.
An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.
Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.
Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.
Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.
FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.
The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.
Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.
“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”
Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.
“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.
Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.
I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.
That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

articles.title: ‘People will have to steer all this AI’: UiPath’s Daniel Dines
articles.text:
UiPath founder and CEO Daniel Dines told customers at FUSION in Dubai on Monday that companies will hand more and more work to AI. People, he said, will have to steer it and answer for what it does. He spoke at the Museum of the Future.
“We need to educate our people to take a lot more initiatives, because we’ll delegate a lot of the work to AI, and I think this is inevitable. But for people, people will have to steer all this AI.” Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO
Dines said today’s education system dates from the industrial revolution, about 200 years ago. Its job was to produce disciplined factory workers who followed orders from the top.
“This is not going to work in the world of AI.” Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO
Companies will need fewer narrow specialists and more people who understand whole systems, he said. He gave lawyers as an example. An AI agent can learn the law from the books, but not how it applies inside a particular company.
Accountability stays with people
Accountability is one of three limits of AI that Dines set out in Las Vegas in September, when UiPath launched Cartographer. The other two are that AI does not learn on the job and that it is not exact.
In Dubai he said that once a company gives AI the autonomy to act, those actions have consequences. Even an email an AI agent sends to a customer can commit the company to something, he said.
“So someone has to bear the consequences.” Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO
He also told companies not to use AI for work that ordinary software can do reliably. Software can be tested, he said, and it gives the same answer every time.
“If AI can do something, it doesn’t mean you have to.” Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO
AI should build that software instead, with people reviewing and testing it before it runs. He drew on the experience of writing his book, The Work That Remains, with AI, where he rarely edited the text himself.
“Believe me, guys, nobody is ever touching the code again.” Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO
Juniors and the Gulf
Dines repeated that companies should keep hiring juniors. They now need to work closely with senior staff from day one and see how decisions are made, he said.
“We have a responsibility for the young generation.” Daniel Dines, UiPath CEO
He called the UAE government “one of the most progressive” he works with on adopting AI and software, and one of UiPath’s best partners.
Karl Crowther, who leads UiPath in the Middle East and Africa, opened the day. He has lived in the UAE for almost 20 years and called its people resilient. The companies that kept core processes running through this year’s disruption were the ones that automated first, he said.
“Automation is almost like a shock absorber for what we’ve experienced.” Karl Crowther, UiPath
Banks, government entities, retailers and oil and gas companies in the UAE are already discussing advanced agentic automation with UiPath, he said.

articles.title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
articles.text:
Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware. Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones.
Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
Anthropic is steering Claude away from re-creating specific titles, but users can still use it to make their own games.
Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.”
Anthropic’s Addy Osmani, in a reply, didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5:
We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.
Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.
We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.
We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well.

articles.title: Quảng Trị gỡ vướng dự án, tăng tốc để đạt tăng trưởng 10,6%
articles.text:
Khoảng 240m mặt bằng còn vướng, liên quan đến đất ở, nhà ở và đất sản xuất của 39 hộ gia đình, là phần việc xã Cửa Việt phải tháo gỡ để thông tuyến đường ven biển kết nối Hành lang kinh tế Đông - Tây trên địa bàn.
Ngày 26/9, khi trực tiếp kiểm tra thực địa tại dự án này và Dự án Cảng hàng không Quảng Trị, Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Quảng Trị Bùi Hoàng Phương yêu cầu địa phương hoàn thành giải phóng mặt bằng trước ngày 30/10. Từ đó, các phần việc tồn đọng được tập trung xử lý, từ rà soát hồ sơ đến hoàn thiện phương án bồi thường, hỗ trợ, tái định cư.
Trao đổi với phóng viên báo VietNamNet, ông Lê Văn Thông, Chủ tịch UBND xã Cửa Việt, cho biết: “Thực hiện chỉ đạo của lãnh đạo tỉnh, địa phương đã huy động nhân lực, tập trung xử lý những phần việc còn tồn đọng. Đến ngày 20/10, công tác giải phóng mặt bằng phục vụ Dự án Cảng hàng không Quảng Trị trên địa bàn đã hoàn thành 100%”.
Với dự án đường ven biển, đến chiều 26/10, các hộ dân đã tiếp nhận và đồng thuận với phương án bồi thường. Theo ông Thông, địa phương dự kiến phê duyệt phương án bồi thường, hỗ trợ, tái định cư đợt cuối vào sáng 27/10, phấn đấu bàn giao mặt bằng trước thời hạn tỉnh giao.
Câu chuyện gỡ vướng tại Cửa Việt cũng cho thấy những công việc Quảng Trị đang phải đẩy nhanh trong những tháng cuối năm. Mỗi phần mặt bằng được bàn giao sẽ tạo điều kiện để các dự án tiếp tục thi công, đưa nguồn vốn đầu tư vào thực tế.
Theo báo cáo tại cuộc họp Đảng ủy UBND tỉnh ngày 29/9, GRDP 9 tháng đầu năm của Quảng Trị ước tăng 8,28%. Trong khi đó, tính đến ngày 17/9, tỷ lệ giải ngân vốn đầu tư công mới đạt 45,66% kế hoạch Thủ tướng Chính phủ giao.
Để đạt mục tiêu tăng trưởng GRDP cả năm 10,6%, tỉnh cần vừa duy trì đà phát triển ở những lĩnh vực có lợi thế, vừa tháo gỡ các vướng mắc đang níu chân dự án. Tiến độ giải phóng mặt bằng tại sân bay và tuyến đường ven biển vì thế là một phần trong nỗ lực khơi thông nguồn lực, tạo thêm động lực tăng trưởng cho địa phương.
Mặt bằng từng bước được bàn giao, yêu cầu tiếp theo là đưa máy móc, nhân lực vào công trường để đẩy nhanh tiến độ tuyến đường ven biển. Quảng Trị yêu cầu chủ đầu tư và các đơn vị thi công tăng cường lực lượng, tổ chức thêm các mũi thi công, tận dụng phần mặt bằng đã có để triển khai công việc.
Với những gói thầu còn chậm hoặc nhà thầu không bảo đảm năng lực, tỉnh yêu cầu nghiên cứu bổ sung nhà thầu phụ. Nội dung này được UBND tỉnh nêu tại văn bản số 4789/UBND-CTXD ngày 30/9, nhằm tăng khả năng thi công trên toàn tuyến.
Theo đại diện Ban Quản lý dự án đầu tư xây dựng công trình Dân dụng, Công nghiệp và Hạ tầng kỹ thuật tỉnh Quảng Trị, đến ngày 20/10, dự án đường ven biển kết nối Hành lang kinh tế Đông - Tây đã được bàn giao 45,67km trong tổng chiều dài 48km mặt bằng, đạt khoảng 95%. Giá trị xây lắp thực hiện đạt 828,789 tỷ đồng trên tổng giá trị 1.615,56 tỷ đồng, tương đương 51,3%.
Mặt bằng đã có phần lớn, nhưng khối lượng xây lắp vẫn còn gần một nửa. Để tuyến đường sớm hình thành, việc tháo gỡ những đoạn còn vướng cần đi cùng với bảo đảm nguồn vật liệu, huy động đủ thiết bị và xử lý kịp thời các khó khăn ngay trên công trường.
Trong lúc các công trình giao thông được thúc tiến độ, những dự án năng lượng cũng mở thêm kỳ vọng tăng trưởng cho Quảng Trị. Ngày 20/10, tại Trung tâm Điện lực Quảng Trạch, EVN phối hợp với UBND tỉnh tổ chức khởi công Nhà máy Nhiệt điện LNG Quảng Trạch II và công bố phát điện Quảng Trạch I lên lưới điện quốc gia.
Phát biểu tại buổi lễ, Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Bùi Hoàng Phương cho rằng Trung tâm Điện lực Quảng Trạch có vai trò tạo động lực, góp phần định hình không gian phát triển công nghiệp của địa phương. Khi vận hành đồng bộ, các nhà máy được kỳ vọng tăng năng lực cung ứng điện và tạo sức lan tỏa cho kinh tế của tỉnh.
Để kỳ vọng ấy thành hiện thực, ông Bùi Hoàng Phương nhấn mạnh trách nhiệm của địa phương trong việc đồng hành với nhà đầu tư. Tỉnh đã phối hợp tháo gỡ vướng mắc về mặt bằng, tái định cư và thủ tục đầu tư; đồng thời cam kết tiếp tục giải quyết kịp thời các khó khăn, chịu trách nhiệm đến cùng với công việc thuộc thẩm quyền.
Gắn trách nhiệm với tiến độ từng dự án
Cùng với các dự án điện gió tại Khe Sanh, những công trình ở Quảng Trạch đang từng bước cụ thể hóa hướng phát triển công nghiệp năng lượng của tỉnh. Từ tuyến đường ven biển đến các nhà máy điện, yêu cầu xuyên suốt vẫn là tháo gỡ từng vướng mắc để dự án có thể triển khai, hoàn thành và đóng góp vào tăng trưởng.
Từ việc gỡ vướng mặt bằng ở Cửa Việt đến cam kết đồng hành cùng các dự án điện tại Quảng Trạch, yêu cầu đặt ra là mỗi công việc phải có người chịu trách nhiệm và thời hạn hoàn thành. Đây cũng là điều Quảng Trị đang tập trung thực hiện để thúc đẩy đầu tư trong những tháng cuối năm.
Ngày 21/10, Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Bùi Hoàng Phương ký công văn số 5214/UBND-TH, yêu cầu lãnh đạo các sở, ban, ngành, địa phương, chủ đầu tư và ban quản lý dự án xác định đẩy nhanh tiến độ thực hiện, giải ngân vốn đầu tư công là nhiệm vụ chính trị trọng tâm trong những tháng còn lại của năm 2026.
Văn bản nêu rõ, chủ đầu tư không giải ngân hết kế hoạch vốn được giao, để dự án bị hủy vốn hoặc mất vốn phải chịu trách nhiệm trước Tỉnh ủy và UBND tỉnh.
Với từng dự án, yêu cầu ấy cần được cụ thể hóa thành những phần việc có thể kiểm đếm: còn bao nhiêu mặt bằng chưa bàn giao, hồ sơ đang vướng ở đâu, đơn vị nào xử lý và khi nào hoàn thành. Khi thời gian giải ngân không còn nhiều, một khâu chậm có thể kéo theo cả công trình chậm tiến độ.
Tại Cửa Việt, chính quyền xã đã phối hợp với các đoàn thể tuyên truyền, vận động những gia đình trong vùng dự án đồng thuận với phương án bồi thường, di dời. Những vướng mắc về mặt bằng từng bước được tháo gỡ, tạo điều kiện để bàn giao cho đơn vị thi công.
Cách làm này cũng cụ thể hóa yêu cầu trong Thông báo kết luận số 443-TB/TU ngày 30/9/2026 của Ban Thường vụ Tỉnh ủy Quảng Trị: chuyển từ hoàn thành thủ tục sang tạo ra kết quả; từ tư duy quản lý sang kiến tạo, phục vụ; không né tránh trách nhiệm; dám nghĩ, dám làm, dám chịu trách nhiệm vì lợi ích chung.
Quảng Trị bước vào quý cuối năm với những kết quả tích cực. Theo báo cáo tại cuộc họp Đảng ủy UBND tỉnh ngày 29/9, thu ngân sách nhà nước ước đạt 8.651 tỷ đồng; chỉ số sản xuất công nghiệp tăng 14,3%; lượng khách du lịch đạt hơn 9,39 triệu lượt, mang lại tổng thu khoảng 10.808 tỷ đồng. Đây là nền tảng để tỉnh tiếp tục theo đuổi mục tiêu tăng trưởng GRDP cả năm 10,6%.
Từ mức tăng 8,28% của 9 tháng đầu năm đến mục tiêu cả năm, chặng đường còn lại đòi hỏi các động lực hiện có tiếp tục được duy trì và nguồn lực đầu tư sớm được đưa vào thực tế. Câu chuyện ở Cửa Việt vì thế gợi ra một yêu cầu cụ thể cho nỗ lực tăng trưởng của Quảng Trị: trách nhiệm phải theo đến từng hồ sơ, từng đoạn mặt bằng, từng mũi thi công. Kết quả cuối cùng cần được nhìn thấy ở những công trình hoàn thành, những cơ hội sản xuất, kinh doanh và việc làm được mở ra cho người dân.

articles.title: Snap settles social media addiction case, sparing Spiegel the stand
articles.text:
Snap has settled with two teenagers who accuse Snapchat and other social media apps of addictive design. Their trial in Los Angeles was days away. The terms are confidential.
Lawyers for the plaintiffs announced the settlement on Monday, Reuters reported. Jury selection began last week. The trial was set to start on Wednesday, according to Hillel Aron of Courthouse News Service.
The plaintiffs had already settled with Meta, TikTok and Google’s YouTube, which left Snap as the last defendant. Courthouse News reported that Snap chief executive Evan Spiegel and Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg were due to testify. It would have been Snap’s first trial in the wider litigation.
The claims
The court identifies the plaintiffs only by their initials. Reuters reported that S.J. is a 16-year-old girl from Illinois. K.D.B. is an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi. They say they started using YouTube as young as 3 and the other apps at around 9.
They blame features such as autoplay and infinite scroll for compulsive use. They say it led to depression, anxiety and eating disorders. The companies reject claims that they built their apps to addict young people.
“What these teenagers need is a permanent fix, real design changes that protect kids, not case-by-case patches,” said plaintiffs’ lawyer Mark Lanier.
In a statement, Snap said both sides were pleased to resolve the matter amicably. The company said it has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and worked with experts.
“Because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community,” Snap said.
Thousands more cases
It was a bellwether case, one of a few drawn from thousands of pending lawsuits to test the claims. In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in the first one. It awarded a young woman $6 million in damages, and both companies have appealed. The next plaintiff’s case ended before trial.
The next bellwether trials are due to start in March, the plaintiffs’ lawyers said. Snap also faces a lawsuit from Pennsylvania over Snapchat’s design.
In August, Meta agreed settlements worth up to $18bn with nearly every US state and territory, Reuters reported. Of that, $5bn depends on the states reaching similar deals with Snap, TikTok and YouTube.
