articles.title: Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure
articles.text:
Xbox’s former chief operating officer, Helen Chiang, suddenly left Microsoft less than two weeks ago after being promoted into the role in July. I wrote in my Notepad newsletter last week that it seemed very weird for Chiang to suddenly depart Microsoft after 21 years with a surprisingly short memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. Now, Chiang says she has “serious concerns” about how she was treated.
Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure
Helen Chiang is setting the record straight on her sudden exit from Microsoft.
In a lengthy LinkedIn post — entitled “Clarity is Kindness,” a reference to Sharma’s WSJ profile — Chiang doesn’t dispute that she was fired, but she doesn’t say why she was let go. Eurogamer reported last month that Chiang had been “terminated for policy violations,” but she says this is “not accurate.”
Chiang denies unfounded rumors that speculated she was leaking confidential information, or that she left to join a competitor. It’s clear the decision to leave Xbox was out of her hands. “You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build,” says Chiang. “Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here.”
She also denies engaging in “discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity.” Like I wrote in Notepad last week, Chiang has been described to me by multiple Xbox employees as highly respected, with high integrity. “I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career,” says Chiang.
The most significant part of Chiang’s post is a paragraph on fairness and accountability, hinting that she wasn’t treated fairly:
I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously.
Chiang also says “This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story.”
We’ve reached out to Chiang to ask if she’s pursuing legal action against Microsoft. We’ve also asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s post, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.

articles.title: Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once | TechCrunch
articles.text:
I never thought I’d get excited about replacing my microwave, but the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer has made a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one. Combining a microwave with a built-in air fryer, it’s designed to speed up everyday cooking, give leftovers their crunch back and, perhaps best of all, free up some valuable kitchen counter space.
Priced at $449.99, it’s certainly not a budget-friendly microwave. But this is no ordinary machine for heating leftover soup. Ninja has paired a 1,000W microwave with a 1,700W air fryer system, powered by its FusionCrisp technology, which combines the speed of microwave cooking with the golden, crispy results you’d typically expect from an air fryer.
Think leftover pizza, chicken tenders, fries, and all those foods that tend to turn sad and soggy in a traditional microwave. Instead, the idea is to get food that’s piping hot and juicy on the inside, with a deliciously crisp, golden finish on the outside. In other words, no more choosing between speed and texture.
Of course, microwave and air fryer combinations aren’t entirely new. Brands such as Smeg have already explored the concept, while plenty of modern microwaves come with a range of additional cooking functions.
What makes the Ninja Crispi Microwave particularly interesting, however, is its FusionCrisp technology, which is designed to bring both cooking methods together rather than simply offering two separate functions. It comes with a 5.5-quart glass cooking dish and a nonstick crisper plate, which sits on top when you want to air fry and crisp up your food.
Another part that makes it stand out is that there isn’t a rotating plate inside, opening up a lot more space to cook more dishes at once.
It’s not just about reheating leftovers. For example, if you want to make a pasta bake, the microwave can cook the pasta, while the air fryer crisps up the cheese on top.
There’s one thing to consider before buying it, though. Measuring 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, the microwave is hardly compact. It takes up a fair amount of counter space, so while it could free up room if you’re replacing a separate microwave and air fryer, it’s not necessarily the ideal solution for a small apartment kitchen.
Then there’s the $449.99 price tag. That’s a considerable amount to spend on a microwave, particularly when a basic model can handle everyday reheating for a fraction of the cost. But if you’re someone who regularly reaches for both a microwave and an air fryer, the combination could make a lot more sense.

articles.title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
articles.text:
In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.
OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters.
The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center.
Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.”
Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.
OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round:
“Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”
OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

articles.title: Northwood Space raises $375M Series C at a $2B valuation from a16z and DFJ Growth | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Space infrastructure company Northwood Space on Monday said it had raised $375 million in a Series C round co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and DFJ Growth, valuing the company at $2 billion.
Founded in 2022, Northwood builds antennas, software, and other technologies that help satellites communicate better with Earth. Bridgit Mendler, co-founder and former actress, serves as its CEO.
The company last raised a $100 million Series B in January, also co-led by Andreessen Horowitz, along with a nearly $50 million contract with the U.S. Space Force to upgrade the nation’s “satellite control network,” TechCrunch previously reported.
This latest round also includes a financial agreement with HSBC that, along with the funding, will be used to scale the company, hire, and fulfill existing contracts, the startup said.

articles.title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
articles.text:
At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.
All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.
A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.
The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.
In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.
The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.
“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”
Hidden Behavior
Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.
“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.
Websites linked to the apps have revealed the network’s secrets and the scale that it operates on. Opening one of the apps’ websites will likely show an entirely black screen and no content. The only noticeable change is that the URL updates to include the word “risk.” But the websites host the hidden explicit deepfake layer that can be loaded in each app.
This web interface contains dozens of pornography deepfake video and image templates—with users able to upload images of people to be added to the sexual scenes. The interface allows the purchase of “diamonds” to generate images and links to other social media accounts where users can contact the developers with questions or complaints.
Also hidden in the websites’ code are details about the entire network. A JavaScript bundle that can easily be unpicked, researchers say, contains a list of all the domains and apps that have been created by the developers—including app package details, encryption keys, Facebook advertising trackers, and more.
“They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys,” says Maël Le Touz, a staff threat researcher at security firm Infoblox, who identified almost 500 linked domains. “They run the same code and they all reference one another.”
Bouchard’s analysis of when domains were registered found that the apps started to appear toward the end of 2025, with a spike during the spring of this year. At one point, around 30 nudify apps-websites were being registered each week, the researcher says, with 27 live on Google’s Play Store in September. These apps had been downloaded more than 350,000 times collectively and many were rated suitable for all age groups, Bouchard’s research says.
One of the most popular apps, called DiffAI, was created in December 2025 and has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store. A user review on Google’s Play Store stated: “This app contains templates for creating CSAM and other types of pornographic material. It performs no age verification.”
DiffAI was removed from the Play Store shortly before WIRED contacted Google about the network. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, though it had removed the majority of the apps ahead of being contacted. (Portions of the deepfake network were reported on by Danish journalists in September.)
Similarly, Apple removed 19 apps from its App Store, including pet photo app Viefur, after WIRED asked the company about the activity and shared associated domains. “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for our users, and nudification apps and other pornographic content are strictly prohibited,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema.
“We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them,” Dema says. “After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.” The company says it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for using these “bait-and-switch” tactics over the last year and recently updated its app store rules to further restrict “nudify” tools.
Chinese Origins
Central to the “nudify” network appears to be a host of Chinese developers whose identities seem to have been intentionally hidden. “It’s using exclusive Chinese hosting, the code is written in Chinese and has a lot of comments in Chinese,” Le Touz says, noting explicit videos in ads posted to Meta’s platforms promoting the apps contained watermarks from Chinese-language video editing software.
The apps and domains across the network have often used generic privacy policies, free email addresses from Gmail or Outlook, and obscure developer names as part of their alleged efforts to hide their connections. Ads for the apps posted on Meta’s platforms have also used apparently false names—such as Draftmondcreldbro Duhustepre and Swaldmungsha Glasirdcroldshold—and pages with no followers. Since the start of this year, Bouchaud’s research has found tens of thousands of explicit deepfake ads linked to the network—often using similar language in their advertising copy—on Meta’s platforms.
“These ads violate not just one, but several of Meta’s policies,” says Katie Paul, the director of the Tech Transparency Project, who first uncovered the ads showing deepfake explicit depictions of minors. “There is no question about what you are seeing, what the app is advertising,” she says. Paul says tech companies need to answer questions about where money generated from the apps goes and how those behind the nudification apps and services constantly seem to bypass their content moderation and safety systems.
KeLing Technology Limited appears to be a significant part of the operation. While the company’s website is little more than a shell, its name was listed as the contact details of the first website registered in the network. This website’s brand name also appeared as part of the contact details within the explicit deepfake template that was used in the apps. Bouchaud also identified an administration login page linked to the explicit deepfake interface that mentions “Keling.” And email addresses using the company’s domain appeared on at least one app that have been removed from app stores.
Towards the end of September, a notification sent to users of the explicit deepfake interface announced that a new AI model could be used—the model was called Veyra, with a tagline in the apps of “More real. More natural. More wild.” The homepage of a website called Veyra AI listed its contact email as a KeLing Technology address.
When WIRED contacted KeLing email addresses, plus some of those listed in apps privacy policies, we received no response. However, after WIRED reached out, someone renamed some of the associated online social media channels, removed KeLing email addresses from the AI Veyra website, and removed the KeLing Technology Limited address from the first registered website.
Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to “comply with a cease and desist letter.” (Meta declined to share the letter with WIRED citing legal reasons.) “We have strict rules against promoting nudify apps and work aggressively to keep this material off our services,” a Meta spokesperson says. Meta says that while KeLing Technology Limited has continued to try and advertise through other ways, it takes action against the ads when it becomes aware of them.
After WIRED shared the 400-plus domains with Meta, the spokesperson said they had shared more than 3,000 associated ads linked to them, two-thirds of which it had already removed from its systems. Meta later told WIRED it has taken action against 11,600 ad accounts, more than 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users, and 15,000 pages linked to the domains, blocking 209 apps from advertising on its platforms.
“The criminals behind them take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection—hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google's and Apple's app stores, with the ads' true intent revealed only after a click,” the spokesperson says.
As WIRED finished reporting this story, similar ads and apps continued to be published on the tech platforms.

articles.title: SUSE to cut about 10% of its workforce, citing AI and automation
articles.text:
SUSE, the German Linux company founded in 1992, is cutting about 10% of its workforce. Chief executive Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told staff on Monday that AI and automation are changing how software companies work.
Liam Proven reported the cuts for The Register, which saw the internal memo. SUSE has more than 1,900 employees, according to its owner, the Swedish private equity firm EQT. That puts the cuts at around 190 people. SUSE has not posted a statement about them in its newsroom.
“What is clear is that automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate,” van Leeuwen wrote.
He wrote that the company’s current structure and cost base will not carry it forward. Modern tooling already lets teams move faster with less overhead and flatter reporting lines, he said.
“The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished,” van Leeuwen wrote.
What happens next
The memo did not say which roles will go. SUSE will tell the staff affected by 4 November, The Register reported. Employee representatives will be nominated the next day, and one-to-one meetings start next week. The rest of the company will see the strategy for fiscal year 2027 on 16 November.
Van Leeuwen called the decisions painful for SUSE’s people, its culture and its open source community. He told staff the cuts reflect changing needs, not their talent or commitment.
In September, The Register reported that SUSE had asked long-serving staff whether they would take voluntary separation.
An owner weighing a sale
Van Leeuwen, a former Red Hat executive, joined SUSE in 2023. EQT bought the Nuremberg company from Micro Focus in 2018 for $2.5bn. It listed SUSE in Frankfurt in 2021 and took it private again in 2023. In March, Reuters reported that EQT was considering selling it.
On 27 October, SUSE announced new agentic AI capabilities for its Linux management tools.
Former SUSE employee Christian Brauner reacted on Mastodon.
“It’s sad that this pointless churn in the name of profit maximizing keeps happening to a great company,” Brauner wrote.
Other employers have tied job cuts to AI in recent weeks. The Netherlands plans to cut 25,000 government jobs. Barclays is cutting 5,000 bank jobs, and American Express is cutting 5% of staff.

articles.title: U.S. reportedly strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance hopes for ‘negotiated settlement’ with Tehran
articles.text:
The U.S. reportedly carried out strikes against Iran on Monday even as Vice President JD Vance expressed hopes of reaching a "negotiated settlement" with Tehran.
America attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, which added that Washington has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks. The military campaign against Iran has been kept quiet on purpose so as not to signal any intention of major combat escalation, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
Qeshm Island, off Iran's southern coast, is the largest island in the Persian Gulf. Located near the Strait of Hormuz, it has emerged as a potential U.S. target amid reports that anti-ship missiles, mines, drones and attack craft are being kept there in underground tunnels.
President Donald Trump's administration has been talking down risks of an all-out war with Iran, with Vance being the latest to claim "good progress" in talks with Iran.
"The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement," Vance told CNN on Monday.
He added, though, that Iranians are "unpredictable" and Trump retains "kinetic and non-kinetic" options against Tehran. Vance said that Washington has not set any deadline for reaching a peace deal with Iran.
Trump said earlier Monday that the U.S. had to go to war with Iran to stop the country from having "a nuclear weapon," that "we're not going to allow Iran ever to have a nuclear weapon. And they understand that."
On Nov. 1, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.

articles.title: CCTV Script 03/11/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on November 03, 2026.
Meta's pursuit of euro denominated bond issuance is driven primarily by cash flow pressures resulting from its expanding artificial intelligence investments. According to its latest earnings report, Meta generated negative 2.1 billion dollars in third quarter free cash flow, marking its first quarter of negative free cash flow since going public in 2012. Additionally, benchmark interest rate differentials between the US and Europe allow Meta to diversify its funding sources while lowering borrowing costs. Benchmark 10 year government bond yields highlight this gap: as of November 2nd, the 10 year US Treasury yield stood at roughly 4.9%, whereas the 10 year German Bund yield traded near 3.3%, representing a 1.6 percentage point spread.
Meta is not the first American tech giant to tap the euro bond market. Alphabet and Amazon have issued a combined total of roughly 29.5 billion euros in euro denominated bonds this year. European debt markets attract these corporations not only through favorable borrowing costs, but also via a deep institutional investor base comprising insurance companies and pension funds. Given the relatively slow expansion of Europe's domestic tech sector, institutional capital increasingly flows toward US cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence initiatives. In essence, European capital markets have served as a financial reservoir for major US tech corporations. A recent European Central Bank report noted that as of August 20th, US tech giants accounted for nearly 10% of all new euro denominated corporate bond issuances by non financial firms.
Industry analysts point out that the influx of major tech issuers provides European bond markets with high quality investment grade paper while expanding portfolio diversification options for investors. However, because institutional capital allocations are finite, investors subscribing to tech bonds may pare back holdings in other corporate or sovereign debt, generating a crowding out effect that pushes up borrowing costs for governments and corporations while elevating credit market risks.
FABRIZIO CAMPELLI
President
Deutsche Bank
"What we're seeing right now in the markets is a concern over an imbalance between supply and demand for debt. Also, we're seeing hyperscalers creating competition with sovereign governments for the issuance of debt, and therefore there would be the necessity to reduce the total stock of debt being held."
Furthermore, select corporations are not only issuing large volumes of debt in European markets, but are also extending bond maturities across decades, and in some cases, a full century. In February of this year, for example, Alphabet issued a 100 year sterling denominated century bond. Analysts warn that given the accelerating pace of technological disruption, ultra long maturities make predicting future operational stability and debt service capacity increasingly difficult, compounding risk evaluation challenges for investors.
Currently, cash flow drain and rising leverage tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure buildouts continue to fuel broad market concern.
SEBASTIAN RAEDLER
Head of European Equity Strategy
Bank of America
"I think the current run rate of the capex is not sustainable. When it deflates, it typically leads to lower asset prices. And I think that's what people should be ready for. Your return on invested capital and your cost of capital, and they're both moving in the wrong direction."
However, White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett stated in an interview with CNBC that the artificial intelligence sector remains well capitalized, dismissing concerns of a systemic selloff.
KEVIN HASSETT
Director of the National Economic Council of the United States
"While sure there are some companies that maybe have a lot of debt, and you kind of worry about there are really, really big pocketed companies, sort of lurking all over the place, owning the equity, owning the debt, perhaps willing to pounce if somebody has trouble."

articles.title: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role
articles.text:
OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company.
Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position.
He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology.
"National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security.
I'm joining OpenAI to help the U.S. and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.Dan DriscollSenior Counselor, OpenAI
The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement.
Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine.
At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program.

articles.title: North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions
articles.text:
North Korea rejected U.S. allegations linking Pyongyang to the estimated $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling the accusation a “grave political provocation,” according to state media.
Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denounced the FBI's attribution of the attack to North Korea-linked hacking group TraderTraitor, Yohnap reported Tuesday, citing the state-run Korean Central News Agency.
"The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said, according to KCNA.
She accused Washington of misleading international public opinion by portraying cybercrimes around the world as the work of North Korea.
The denial comes as blockchain analytics firms trace billions of dollars in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through thousands of wallets across multiple blockchains.
Elliptic and Chainalysis said hackers linked to North Korea have used increasingly complex techniques to obscure the trail of the funds.
In the first four days after the attack, the hackers used roughly 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains and conducted more than 40,000 transactions, Elliptic said in a report Monday. The activity appeared highly complex and automated, with an average of one new wallet used every 25 seconds.
Much of the laundering activity initially took place on the Tron blockchain, where stolen funds were distributed across about 7,700 addresses before being moved to Ethereum through cross-chain bridges, according to Elliptic. At least $147 million had been transferred out of Tron through such bridges.
The hackers also used decentralized exchanges to swap stolen stablecoins into cryptocurrencies that cannot be frozen by their issuers, including ether. Elliptic said roughly $786 million in stablecoins was converted before issuers including Tether and Circle froze the remaining assets.
The laundering operation has since expanded to other blockchains, including Solana. Chainalysis said North Korea-linked actors had begun a new phase of laundering after moving more than $500 million through intermediary wallets on Tron.
Elliptic also identified the first signs of bitcoin mixing, a technique designed to make transactions harder to trace. About 28 bitcoin, worth $2.2 million, had passed through 18 mixing transactions as of early Monday, the firm said.
Despite the extensive movement of funds, about $2.85 billion — or 44% of exactly $6.43 billion stolen as reported by Elliptic — has been frozen or seized, while roughly $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly in bitcoin and ether.
The firm said only a negligible amount of stolen funds appeared to have been cashed out, with most of the activity involving transfers or conversions between cryptocurrencies rather than exchanges into spendable funds.
Elliptic said the laundering has moved slower than after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, when North Korean hackers moved all the stolen ether within 10 days. It expects the remaining funds to be gradually converted into bitcoin and potentially cashed out through over-the-counter brokers and exchanges over several months.
Binance, meanwhile, said withdrawals were resuming in phases and warned users against scammers offering to expedite transactions or help claim compensation.
The exchange added it has covered about 95% of the affected amount, with the remaining 5% consisting of less liquid tokens that take longer to source. Binance said it was working with industry partners to acquire the remaining assets.

articles.title: Apple's quarter is not perfect. But with enough to like, we raised our price target
articles.text: Apple shares fell Monday evening after the iPhone maker delivered a better-than-expected quarter but offered mixed guidance due to a slowdown in services revenue growth and high memory costs eating into margins. Revenue in Apple's fiscal 2026 fourth quarter ended Sept. 26 increased 12% to $114.48 billion, ahead of the $113.39 billion expected, according to LSEG. Earnings per share (EPS) grew 14% to $2.10, ahead of estimates of $1.99, according to LSEG. Bottom line We remain "own it, don't trade it" on Apple stock. Shares entered the print on a tear year to date. During an October in which tech stocks were hammered by concerns over AI funding, Apple stood out, hitting a new all-time high late in the month. Apple has emerged as a relative winner in the market as the data center trade has come under pressure. AAPL YTD mountain Apple YTD Shares entered Monday evening up 25% year to date, outperforming Amazon , Alphabet , Meta Platforms , and Microsoft (all fellow Club holdings). While hyperscalers are burning through much of their free cash flow to fund AI investments, with Microsoft a notable exception, Apple continues to generate substantial positive FCF. That allowed Apple to repurchase $24 billion worth of stock in the quarter and $86 billion over the past 12 months. The rally pushed the stock's valuation to over 35 times next 12 months' EPS estimates, its highest level in recent memory. That meant the company needed to report a picture-perfect quarter with a strong outlook to avoid profit-taking. Unfortunately, that did not happen. However, Apple's quarterly results were strong, with revenue, gross margin upside, and Services about in line. The figures were enough to keep the stock unchanged for most of the evening. However, when management provided guidance for the current quarter, the stock fell about 3% in after-hours trading due to downside in gross margins and Services revenue growth relative to Street expectations. The company's overall revenue guide was better than expected. Apple has managed through rising memory costs for several quarters now, and prices aren't easing anytime soon. December's memory costs are expected to be higher than September's, which was up from the June quarter. Memory costs are outside management's control and won't remain this high forever, so our focus is on how Apple is navigating the issue. One way they can offset these higher costs is by raising prices, as it did with Macs and iPads in June and iPhones in September. Apple is also pursuing lower costs on non-memory components. What is in the company's control is the products and services it introduces, and it appears they have a hit with the launch of the foldable iPhone Duo. The new form factor sold out immediately on its launch date, a sign that there isn't enough supply to meet the demand. "iPhone Duo is constrained as of today," Apple COO Sabih Khan confirmed on the earnings call. "The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance." The Duo was available for preorder Oct. 16 and hit stores on Oct. 23. So, none of the revenue from the new device was included in the September quarter numbers. There was no mention of the reports of cracks in Duo screens on the earnings call, which Apple previously acknowledged. The company has said the issue impacted a "small number" of devices and that affected users "should contact AppleCare for a replacement." From an AI perspective, CEO John Ternus, on his first earnings call since succeeding Tim Cook on Sept. 1, emphasized the iPhone's role as "the intelligent personal hub" and Siri AI's ability to tap into the wealth of personal information stored on the device. "If you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that," he explained. "Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private and that nobody else has access to." We come away balanced from the quarter, understanding that Apple continues to gain share over its competitors in the smartphone and PC markets while memory costs remain a temporary challenge. We're raising our price target slightly to $360 from $340 per share but keeping our hold-equivalent 2 rating due to the run it has had and lofty valuation. Quarterly commentary Products revenue increased 12.5 year over year to $82.9 billion, outpacing the $82.26 billion estimate. The better-than-expected result was driven by the 17.5% growth in iPhone and 24% growth in Mac sales. The Mac outperformance is notable given the personal computer market warning Intel gave last week. Wearables, Home & Accessories sales fell 8% year over year, but that was better than feared. iPad sales declined 10.4% year over year, worse than analyst expectations. Services revenue growth decelerated sequentially, just below 10% year over year. Sales of $31.57 billion were just shy of estimate of $31.59 billion. But the company remains upbeat about the future growth of its services business, thanks to the large install base of over 2.5 billion active devices it can monetize. Company-wide gross margin came in at the high end of management's outlook, improving 70 basis points year over year to 47.9%. That beat the consensus forecast of 47.5%. The result included a favorable impact of 1 percentage point from tariff refunds. Excluding the tariff refund, gross margins would have been down one percentage point sequentially, primary due to higher memory costs. By unit , Products gross margin improved 100 basis points year over year to 37.2%, beating the analyst forecast of 36.8%. Services profitability made up for the slight revenue shortfall, with gross margin expanding 70 basis points year over year to 76%, beating analyst forecasts of 75.1%. By region , Apple had double-digit growth in every region except Japan, where sales slipped by about 1%. Despite longstanding concerns about competition, the Greater China region delivered the strong year on year growth at 21%. Apple topped the consensus forecast in Greater China as well as Europe and the Rest of Asia Pacific. The Americas and Japan were small misses. Guidance Taking a closer look at Apple's current quarter guidance, the holiday quarter that is the company's fiscal 2027 first quarter. December quarter revenue is expected to increase by 7% to 10% versus the year-ago period, above the 5.8% growth the Street was looking for, according to FactSet. This works out to a revenue guide of $155.98 billion versus the consensus of $152.12 billion. That was the good news. The bad news was that the high-margin Services revenue growth is expected to slow down again. The company guided Services revenue growth to 8% to 9%, below the Street estimate of 10%. This works out to a guide of $32.56 billion versus the consensus estimate of $33 billion. The combination of a higher mix of hardware sales (lower margin) with the ongoing memory price increase are probably the reasons why the gross margin guide was light. The company guided gross margin between 45% to 46% which is below is below the consensus estimate of 46.9%, Apple also called out a step up in inference costs in connection to Siri AI. articles.title: Jim Cramer says these six fashion stocks are buys beyond the AI trade
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer highlighted six fashion and apparel stocks on Monday for investors looking for alternatives to the struggling AI trade.
While technology stocks have come under pressure in recent weeks, consumer stocks have been resilient. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) gained 10% this quarter, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) fell 11%. Cramer said falling interest rates could provide an additional boost to apparel companies heading into the holiday shopping season.
"Ralph Lauren, Tapestry, Levi's, VF Corp, Kontoor Brands and Reformation are some of the fashion stocks that we think look best right now," the "Mad Money" host said.
Ralph Lauren remains Cramer's favorite apparel stock, thanks to its consistent growth under CEO Patrice Louvet. The company has continued gaining momentum across women's apparel, accessories and outerwear, and has been strengthening its international presence, particularly in Asia. Although the stock pulled back in August and September, it has since recovered, and Cramer is optimistic ahead of Thursday morning's earnings report.
Tapestry, the parent of Coach and Kate Spade, also reports Thursday. Cramer likes Coach's position in the accessible luxury market, particularly its popularity among younger female consumers. However, shares have fallen 20% since the company's August earnings report, when guidance failed to impress investors following a massive multiyear rally. "I hope this Thursday's report can represent the start of a comeback for Tapestry," he said.
Levi Strauss is another potential turnaround story. Shares fell below $20 following disappointing earnings a few weeks ago, but CEO Michelle Gass told Cramer that the company had moved quickly to address inventory shortages in popular styles. The stock has since rebounded more than 20% from its post-earnings low, though Cramer still considers it inexpensive at roughly 14 times earnings, with a 2.8% dividend yield. "I think this is a good option to play the broader strength in denim that we keep hearing about," he said.
VF Corp, which owns The North Face, Vans and Timberland, is showing signs of improvement after years of struggles, particularly at Vans. Cramer pointed to encouraging results from a recent Piper Sandler teen survey and a strong quarterly report as evidence that the sneaker brand's turnaround may be gaining traction. Shares have risen roughly 14% since he recommended the stock about two weeks ago.
Kontoor Brands offers another opportunity tied to denim and corporate restructuring. The company plans to sell its Lee brand for up to $1 billion, allowing it to focus on Wrangler and outdoor apparel maker Helly Hansen. Cramer expects the sale to be followed by substantial share repurchases and said the remaining businesses have room to grow. Shares trade at roughly 14 times earnings and offer a dividend yield near 3%.
Cramer's more speculative pick is Reformation. The women's fashion brand initially struggled after its IPO in late July, but Cramer said it "has great growth, it's profitable, and it has a differentiated shopping experience with a technology kicker." Cramer highlighted the stock in late September; shares surged more than 31% in October.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says lower oil prices are giving stocks a boost. Can it last?
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer said that lower oil prices and Treasury yields are fueling a broader stock market rally.
Brent crude tumbled 7.63% Monday to close at $104.77 per barrel, sending the 10-year Treasury yield to its lowest level since Sept. 10. That helped lift shares across the healthcare, financials, retail and travel sectors. Cramer said the improved market backdrop has prompted investors to revisit strong earnings reports they initially overlooked and accelerated the shift toward growth opportunities beyond tech.
"Never forget what this market's really about: oil, inflation and interest rates," the "Mad Money" host said. "Oil plummeted overnight ... which sent interest rates lower and caused a host of stocks to soar."
Cramer pointed to Amazon, up 2% Monday, as an example of how falling rates can change investors' perceptions of a stock. Shares recovered after initially struggling following the company's quarterly report last week. Cramer argued that Amazon's results were stronger than the market initially recognized, and "sure enough, with a better rate backdrop we saw Amazon return to where it was in late September."
Similarly, Waste Management gained 1.8% as investors finally gave the company credit for the strong quarterly results last week, which Cramer said had been overshadowed by rising rates.
Still, Cramer cautioned that the magnitude of these moves may be difficult to sustain. "You just have money piling into stocks at the same time," he said. "They aren't sustainable."
But with investors continuing to move money out of technology while remaining invested in the broader market, Cramer said companies in other industries could increasingly take the lead. "These are the new proxies for growth as tech continues to lose its luster," he said.
The rally extended to medical device makers, which Cramer said are emerging as attractive alternatives. Medtronic gained 3% Monday, while GE HealthCare rose 4% and Intuitive Surgical climbed 1%. "If you can find a growth stock that's not a tech stock, you can really clean up," Cramer said.
Financial stocks also rallied as worries about consumers' ability to repay debt eased. Capital One jumped 3% after struggling last week amid worries about higher gasoline prices and credit delinquencies.
The gains lifted consumer companies, with Walmart and Costco each rising roughly 3%. "Rates lower and gasoline lower means more [money] to spend inside their stores," he said.

articles.title: S&P 500 futures are flat as investors weigh Apple earnings; U.S. midterm elections loom: Live updates
articles.text:
S&P 500 futures were little changed on Monday night as investors mulled over Apple's quarterly earnings report and awaited U.S. midterm elections.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures gained 24 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.1%. Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.3%.
Apple shares were down 2% in extended trading after the consumer tech giant rolled out a disappointing margin forecast and iPad sales in the fiscal fourth quarter missed the Street's estimates.
Over in Asia, markets were mixed on Tuesday, with South Korea's Kospi tracking the tech losses on Wall Street.
The benchmark index slipped 3.28% in early trade, with heavyweight Samsung Electronics down 4.37%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200, on the other hand, still was in positive territory, up 0.22%.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.16% in early trade in Asia, with gains in the academic and education sector offsetting losses from the energy sector.
Mainland China, on the other hand, saw the CSI 300 index slip 0.84%, weighed down by tech and energy stocks.
Japan's markets are closed for a public holiday.
In the regular U.S. session, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dipped 1.07%, while the S&P 500 fell 0.51% as investors continued their rotation out of tech stocks. The Dow rose about 214 points, or 0.41%.
Marvell Technology shares fell about 12%, while Lumentum dropped 18% after Marvell announced it would acquire Lumentum in a $115 billion deal. Oracle shares also fell 8% after the company said it plans to sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in bonds to help finance its artificial intelligence build-out.
As Tuesday approaches, investors will turn their attention toward the midterm elections, where prediction market traders see a nearly 75% likelihood of Democrats taking the Senate. A sweep of the House and Senate by Democrats could spark a sell-off for artificial intelligence stocks, according to JPMorgan.
Even with President Donald Trump in the White House, a victory by Democrats in either the House or Senate could shape investigations and oversight in Washington — which is key for industries like defense, artificial intelligence and healthcare.
Once the elections are over, markets may find some calm, according to Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group. "There's some anxiousness before these elections," he told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
However, an outright sweep by either party could shake up stocks. "If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Tuesday will be a busy day for investors packed with a raft of corporate earnings. Pfizer, Shopify, Eaton and Marathon Petroleum are among those scheduled to release results before the open, followed by Advanced Micro Devices and Super Micro Computer in the afternoon.
On the economic front, traders await the release of the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey for September, as well as factory orders data.

articles.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Nvidia's humanoid push relies on China-made robot hands
articles.text:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Chinese robot companies still underpin many U.S. tech endeavors, especially when it comes to the pain point of robotic hands. Who is one of the latest on Nvidia's radar?
The big story
In just a few months, Nvidia has showcased two humanoid robot training packages: one with mechanical hands from Sharpa, and another with hands from Wuji.
Both have ties to founders in Shanghai.
Pan Yunzhe founded Wuji in 2019, eventually moving much of the team to Shenzhen and drawing backers such as Ant Group, HSG and Future Capital, according to PitchBook. A demo video last week claimed a Wuji Hand 2 could autonomously spin a pen, despite interference.
The Wuji Hand 2 made it onto a slide Oct. 21 behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as he told a crowd in Berlin about a new humanoid hardware system for training the robots on Nvidia software. The robot body comes from Agile Robots, which has offices in Germany, China and the U.S.
"It will be the flywheel by which we can accelerate development of robotics," Huang said of the hardware system, called Agile One SN. Agile Robots announced the system, which uses Nvidia's Isaac robotics software and Jetson Thor computing platform.
Research institutions, such as Stanford and ETH Zurich, can likely start using the Agile One SN system in early 2027, according to Nvidia.
Stanford and ETH Zurich were also among the institutions Nvidia named in connection with its first reference humanoid design, announced May 31. That system uses a body from Chinese humanoid company Unitree and mechanical hands from Sharpa. It was scheduled for delivery from late 2026.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether deliveries had begun, or whether the researchers would try both reference robots, or just one.
Sharpa, headquartered in Singapore, was co-founded by David Li, CEO of Shanghai-based lidar company Hesai. Sharpa has said its manufacturing R&D is in Shanghai.
While these are just two of the many robotic hand makers in China — and globally — they've grown so much in prominence that Google DeepMind research lead Keerthana Gopalakrishnan directly compared the two startups in a podcast last month.
Sharpa Wave is a bit stronger than Wuji, which is closer in size to a typical human hand but has the strength of a ten-year-old, she said. It was not clear whether she was testing the Wuji Hand 2 or an earlier version.
In September, humanoid startup JoyIn's Zhu Mingxuan told me she found Wuji's mechanical hands very light and very good at completing tasks, but prone to heating up while doing so. She said Sharpa's performed better, but were far more expensive.
Hardware is limiting humanoid development, and hands are the main challenge, she said. Zhu said she left U.S. humanoid company Figure last year, where she had also worked on models to help humanoid robots mimic human actions.
As China pushes its humanoid industry to develop more core technologies, mechanical hands are one way companies can try to stand out in the robot race.
Consumer electronics company Xiaomi said last week that, by testing its robotic hand in its car factory, it found that most of the tasks it tested required only a specific range of movement.
And in another sign of just how far along the tech may have come in China, Meta has worked with Chinese startup Fourier for a humanoid prototype, The Information reported Oct. 31, citing sources. Neither company immediately responded to a request for comment.
Need to know
Why China is desperate to ship cars outside of the country
Car salesman Li Ke said that, other than the Covid-19 pandemic, the "golden September and silver October" season is the slowest this year he's seen in his 26 years on the job.
China industrial profits see strongest growth since June
Profits at large industrial firms rose 14.4% in September from a year earlier, according to official data.
Labubu-maker Pop Mart's shares extend declines as sales plunge
The company reported a 45% to 50% year-on-year drop in third-quarter revenue, with the Americas and Asia-Pacific seeing the steepest sales drops.

articles.title: Kimberly-Clark closes its acquisition of Tylenol maker Kenvue. What to expect next
articles.text: Kimberly-Clark on Monday completed its blockbuster acquisition of Tylenol maker Kenvue, giving investors new reasons to believe in the company behind Huggies, Kleenex and Cottonelle. The acquisition broadens Kimberly-Clark's reach into the health and wellness category, at a time when consumers are placing a greater emphasis on healthy lifestyles. And it's a major reason why Jim Cramer added the stock to the Club's portfolio in early September . We've since added to the position three times, including twice in October below $98 a share. Shares of Kimberly-Clark rose 0.3% in Monday's session, closing at $108.25. With the stock's strong performance of late, Jim said on Monday's Morning Meeting he would wait for weakness before looking to buy more shares. The Kenvue takeover closed almost a year to the day that it was announced , valuing the company at almost $49 billion when including debt. On Monday, Kimberly-Clark reaffirmed its financial goals for the deal, including $1.9 billion in reduced costs and expenses within three years. It also includes $500 million in incremental profits resulting from increased revenue, partially offset by $300 million in reinvestments. Still, there are lingering questions about how Kimberly-Clark will integrate Kenvue, navigate higher input costs, and manage the legal troubles surrounding popular over-the-counter pain reliever, Tylenol. Kimberly-Clark CEO Michael Hsu joined Jim on CNBC earlier Monday, where he laid out his vision for the combined company moving forward and addressed these key debates. Accelerating Kenvue's growth One of Kimberly-Clark's biggest priorities is to accelerate growth at Kenvue by strengthening key pieces of the business. Jim has previously pointed out weakness in Kenvue's operations, particularly its e-commerce strategy, which creates an opportunity for Kimberly-Clark to step in and make improvements. "We've been really focused the last 10 years at [Kimberly-Clark] to fundamentally build what I kind of term world-class CPG capability," Hsu said, using an abbreviation for consumer packaged goods, or everyday products that consumers regularly use and replace. Those efforts have included strengthening Kimberly-Clark's relationships with retailers, digital capabilities, advertising and product innovation. Though Kimberly-Clark's work isn't done in these areas, Hsu said the company is on stronger footing than Kenvue. Previously the consumer health division of Johnson & Johnson, Kenvue was spun out into a stand-alone company in May 2023. "I still would say we're in the early innings of developing that capability, but I think we're further along than Kenvue," Hsu said. "And I think [by] combining, we can bring some of those capabilities together and help us accelerate growth." Hsu also sees considerable room for expansion across Kenvue's existing product categories, which he described as "very, very underdeveloped." Besides Tylenol, Kenvue's brands include Band-Aid, Zyrtec, Neutrogena and Listerine. "There's a lot of growth left in those hills," he said. KMB YTD mountain Kimberly-Clark's year-to-date stock performance. Dealing with inflation Kimberly-Clark also has another challenge on its hands: managing higher input costs due to the Iran war, while keeping prices affordable for cash-strapped lower- and middle-income consumers. Hsu acknowledged that it's a delicate balancing act, given the risk that high prices could turn customers toward cheaper alternatives. Nevertheless, Hsu painted the current situation as manageable, particularly considering what Kimberly-Clark faced coming out of the Covid-19 pandemic, when the U.S. inflation rate surged to multi-decade highs. "Back in post-Covid, the inflation that we took on, just in Kimberly-Clark, was about $3.4 billion over two years," Hsu said. "We're talking, at this point, between the two companies combined, a few hundred million. While it's significant, we know how to navigate this." Hsu said the company generally aims to offset higher commodity costs through pricing over time. "We're very sensitive to the plight of the average consumer. We know middle-income and lower-income consumers are cash strapped, trying to make difficult choices. They're very discerning," Hsu said. For Hsu, this means maintaining price discipline. "More importantly, I think we're really focused on reducing our cost so that we can afford to provide great products at an affordable price." In touting Kimberly-Clark's focus on value, Hsu mentioned the company recently brought some innovation to its value-tier Huggies Snug & Dry. The technology improves softness in the diapers. "We put our best technology into our value tier diaper," Hsu said. "We know consumers really value performance and they're very discerning about it. And that's where we want to earn the trust of the average consumer. " Tylenol's legal troubles In acquiring Kenvue, Kimberly-Clark also inherits legal and reputational risks over Tylenol, which has faced litigation and controversy over allegations concerning its use during pregnancy. Back in July, a federal appeals court resurrected more than 500 lawsuits that alleged prenatal Tylenol use contributed to autism or ADHD in children, citing improper exclusion of expert testimony. Kenvue fought the decision, but about two weeks ago, a U.S. appeals court said it wouldn't reconsider the ruling. Hsu defended the pain and fever reliever, saying Kimberly-Clark conducted extensive research and consulted with medical and legal experts as it pursued the acquisition. In September 2025, more than a month before Kimberly-Clark announced the Kenvue deal, the Trump administration drew an unproven link between autism and pregnant women's use of the active ingredient in Tylenol, acetaminophen. Shares of Kenvue got crushed that month and continued sliding through October. Then the takeover was unveiled. "Our perspective is the science supporting the efficacy and the safety of Tylenol has been proven out, I think, consistently, even with multiple new studies coming out over the past year," Hsu said. "We feel really good that we stand on the right side of science." Hsu said the elevated controversy in 2025 had a "modest" impact on Tylenol sales at that time, but he argued that the brand has recovered and has momentum on its side. He pointed to recent consumption data up double-digits. Hsu also highlighted Tylenol with Naproxen , which in July became the first and only FDA-approved over-the-counter pain reliever combining acetaminophen and naproxen sodium. Aleve, which is owned by Germany's Bayer, is a brand name of naproxen sodium. Protecting the dividend and balance sheet Kimberly-Clark's dividend is another reason that Jim likes the stock. The company is a "dividend aristocrat," meaning it has increased its dividend payout for at least 25 consecutive years. In fact, it actually belongs to more rarefied "dividend king" territory, having boosted its payout for at least 50 years in a row. Based on Monday's close, the stock has a dividend yield of 4.73%. With Kimberly-Clark issuing some debt to help fund the cash-and-stock Kenvue takeover, Jim asked Hsu whether the company's dividend was safe. Hsu was quick to assure investors that it is. "Oh, yeah," Hsu responded. That commitment is particularly important for income-focused investors who have long viewed Kimberly-Clark as a reliable dividend-paying stock. "We believe we're going to create generational value creation on shareholder friendly terms," Hsu said. "I think by year two, we expect earnings to be accretive and to reduce our leverage back to about 2.0," Hsu added. "And so our goal is ... we're going to maintain our dividend aristocracy." Hsu also said Kimberly-Clark intends to maintain its single-A credit rating. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long KMB. See here for a full list of the stocks.)
